title.raw: What to Expect When You Get an X-Ray at Our Lufkin Facility
title.rendered: What to Expect When You Get an X-Ray at Our Lufkin Facility

content.raw:
If you or a loved one has recently been injured or is dealing with a persistent cough, your healthcare provider may have recommended an X-ray. It is perfectly natural to feel a bit of "white-coat" anxiety when a diagnostic test is ordered. However, an X-ray is one of the oldest, safest, and most effective tools available to help our team in Lufkin understand exactly what is happening inside your body. At our facility, we believe that clear communication is the first step toward healing. This guide will walk you through the entire process from preparation to results so you can feel confident and cared for during your visit.

What Exactly is an X-Ray?

An X-ray is a quick, painless medical test that helps physicians view the structures inside your body. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), X-rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation, much like visible light, but with higher energy that allows them to pass through most objects, including the body. When these beams pass through you, they are absorbed in different amounts depending on the density of the material they encounter. This is why the resulting image looks like a black-and-white photograph:
  • Bones and Teeth: These are very dense and absorb the most radiation, appearing bright white.
  • Soft Tissues: Fat and muscle absorb less, appearing in various shades of gray.
  • Lungs: Because they are filled with air, they absorb the least radiation and appear black.

Why Might You Need an X-Ray?

While most people associate X-rays with broken bones, they are used for a wide variety of diagnostic purposes. Our Lufkin team utilizes X-ray technology to:
  1. Identify Fractures and Infections: In most cases, bone fractures and infections show up clearly on an image.
  2. Monitor Joint Health: X-rays can reveal signs of arthritis or help doctors track if the condition is progressing.
  3. Chest and Lung Evaluation: A chest X-ray is often the first step in diagnosing pneumonia, a collapsed lung, or an enlarged heart.
  4. Locate Swallowed Objects: For our younger patients, X-rays are vital in finding small metal objects that may have been accidentally swallowed.

Preparing for Your Visit to Our Lufkin Facility

Preparation for a standard X-ray is minimal, which is one of the reasons it is such a preferred diagnostic tool in urgent care settings.

What to Wear

In general, you should wear comfortable, loose-fitting clothing. Depending on the area being examined, you may be asked to change into a medical gown. The UCSF Radiology Department notes that you should remove any metal objects, such as jewelry, eyeglasses, or piercings, as metal can block the X-ray beam and interfere with the clarity of the image.

Important Health Notifications

Before the procedure begins, it is essential to notify your technologist if:
  • You are pregnant: While the risk to a fetus is generally very low for most X-rays, the CDC recommends taking special precautions or considering alternative imaging like an ultrasound if you are or may be pregnant.
  • Recent Barium Studies: If you have had a recent "contrast" study (like a barium swallow), let your provider know, as the contrast material may still be in your system and could show up on the scan.

The X-Ray Procedure: Step-by-Step

When you arrive at our Lufkin facility, you will be greeted by a Radiologic Technologist. These are healthcare professionals specially trained to operate the equipment and ensure you are positioned safely and accurately.
  1. Positioning: You may be asked to stand, sit, or lie down on an X-ray table. The technologist might use pillows or sandbags to help you maintain the correct position.
  2. Shielding: To follow safety protocols, a lead apron or "shield" may be placed over your lap or chest to protect sensitive organs from unnecessary exposure.
  3. Staying Still: Much like a regular camera, movement can cause the image to be blurry. You may be asked to hold your breath for a second or two while the image is being captured.
  4. Duration: Most routine X-rays take only a few minutes. You won't feel anything as the X-ray beams pass through your body.

A Note on Safety and Radiation

It is normal to have questions about radiation. However, it is important to put the exposure into perspective. The FDA explains that the amount of radiation used in a standard diagnostic X-ray is very small. For example, a single chest X-ray provides a dose of radiation roughly equal to what you would naturally receive from the environment (sunlight, soil, etc.) over the course of about 10 days. At our facility, we strictly follow the ALARA principle, which stands for "As Low As Reasonably Achievable." This means we use the minimum amount of radiation necessary to get a high-quality diagnostic image.

After the Exam: Understanding Your Results

Once the images are captured, your part is done! You can immediately return to your normal daily activities. The images are sent to a Radiologist, a specialized doctor who interprets medical images. They will analyze the "shades of gray" to look for abnormalities and send a formal report to your primary doctor. Your doctor will then contact you to discuss the findings and plan any necessary follow-up care. According to NIH, in some cases, additional views or a different type of scan might be recommended to get a more detailed look.

Need an X-ray? Get it Done Today!

If you're dealing with injuries, persistent pain, or other concerns, our team at the ER of Lufkin can help. Get your X-ray quickly and safely to understand what's happening inside your body. Don’t wait, schedule your appointment now! Visit the ER of Lufkin now for fast relief and expert care. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Does an X-ray hurt? 

No. The X-ray itself is completely painless. You cannot feel the radiation as it passes through your body.

How long will I have to wait for results? 

In many urgent care or emergency settings, results are available relatively quickly. However, a final report from a radiologist typically takes 24 to 48 hours to be sent to your referring physician.

Can I stay in the room with my child? 

Usually, yes. If your child is the one getting the X-ray, you can often stay to provide comfort. You will be asked to wear a lead apron to protect yourself from any "scatter" radiation.

Do I need to fast before an X-ray? 

For most routine X-rays of the bones or chest, no fasting is required. However, for specific X-rays involving the digestive tract (like a GI series), you may be asked to avoid eating or drinking for several hours prior.

Is the radiation dangerous? 

The benefits of an accurate diagnosis generally far outweigh the very small risk associated with the low dose of radiation used in a diagnostic X-ray.

What if I am pregnant? 

You must inform your technologist. While many X-rays (like those of the extremities or chest) can be done safely with shielding, your doctor may decide to postpone the test or use an alternative like an ultrasound.

Does an X-ray hurt?

How long will I have to wait for results?

title.raw: “I Touched Poison Ivy”: How to Treat the Rash and When to Get Help
title.rendered: “I Touched Poison Ivy”: How to Treat the Rash and When to Get Help

content.raw:
We’ve all been there: a weekend hike, a quick afternoon of gardening, or a game of fetch with the dog that ends with the realization that you just brushed against "leaves of three." If you suspect you’ve touched poison ivy, that familiar prickle of anxiety can be just as uncomfortable as the itch itself. You’re likely wondering: How bad is this going to get? How do I stop the spread? When should I be worried? At our clinic, we see patients every day dealing with the aftermath of an encounter with nature. While a poison ivy rash is rarely life-threatening, it can be incredibly disruptive to your sleep, work, and quality of life. Understanding how to manage the reaction and knowing exactly when to seek professional medical help is the best way to get back to feeling like yourself.

What Actually Happens When You Touch Poison Ivy?

It isn’t the plant itself that causes the rash, but an oily resin called urushiol. This oil is found in the leaves, stems, and roots of poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac. According to the FDA, urushiol is incredibly potent. It stays active on surfaces like gardening tools, clothing, or pet fur for months or even years. When it touches your skin, it triggers an allergic reaction called allergic contact dermatitis. 

Immediate First Aid: What to Do in the First 30 Minutes

If you know you’ve just made contact, the clock is ticking. You have a small window to remove the oil before it binds to your skin.

1. Wash the Skin Immediately

Rinse your skin with lukewarm, soapy water. The CDC recommends using a degreasing soap (like dish soap) or a specialized poison ivy wash if available. Scrubbing isn't necessary; gentle, thorough washing is key to lifting the oil away.

2. Clean Everything Else

Urushiol is "sticky." If you touched the plant, the oil is now on your clothes, your shoelaces, and perhaps your gardening gloves. Throw your clothes into the washing machine on a hot cycle. According to Medline, if your pet were with you, they may need a bath (use pet shampoo and wear rubber gloves) because they can carry the oil on their fur and transfer it to you later.

Identifying the Poison Ivy Rash: What Does it Look Like?

The rash typically doesn't appear the second you touch the plant. It usually develops within 12 to 48 hours after exposure. Common symptoms include:
  • Intense itching (often the first sign).
  • Redness and swelling.
  • Blisters, which may be small or large and often form in a straight line (where the plant brushed against you).
  • Crusting as the blisters begin to heal.
A common myth is that the fluid inside the blisters spreads the rash. According to the NIH, the blister fluid is just your body’s natural reaction and does not contain urushiol. You cannot spread the rash to another person or another part of your body once the oil has been washed off your skin.

At-Home Treatments for Relief

If the rash is mild and confined to a small area, you can often manage the discomfort at home. The goal is to reduce the itch so you don't scratch, as scratching can lead to a bacterial infection.

Soothing Baths and Compresses

  • Cool Compresses: Apply a cold, damp cloth to the area for 15 to 20 minutes several times a day.
  • Oatmeal Baths: Soaking in a lukewarm bath with a colloidal oatmeal treatment can significantly calm inflamed skin.
  • Baking Soda: Adding a cup of baking soda to bathwater is another FDA-suggested remedy for itching.

Over-the-Counter (OTC) Solutions

  • Calamine Lotion: This classic remedy helps dry up weeping blisters.
  • Hydrocortisone Cream: A 1% hydrocortisone cream can reduce swelling and redness for mild cases.
  • Oral Antihistamines: While they won't "cure" the rash, medicines like diphenhydramine can help you sleep if the itching is keeping you awake.

The "Don’ts" of Poison Ivy Care

  • Don't Scratch: Breaking the skin with your fingernails introduces bacteria, which can lead to a secondary infection.
  • Don't Pop Blisters: Leave them intact to act as a natural bandage for the raw skin underneath.
  • Don't Use Hot Water: While hot water might feel "good" on an itch momentarily, it can increase inflammation and irritate sensitive skin further.

When to See a Doctor: Signs of a Severe Reaction

Sometimes, home remedies aren't enough. If your reaction is widespread or causing significant distress, professional medical intervention is necessary. You should book an appointment at an urgent care or see your primary doctor if:
  • The rash covers more than 25% of your body.
  • The rash is on your face, eyes, mouth, or genitals.
  • You have widespread blisters that are leaking a lot of fluid.
  • The itching is so severe that you cannot sleep or perform daily tasks.
  • You develop a fever, or the rash starts to look infected (pus, increasing pain, or warmth).
Doctors can prescribe stronger topical steroids or a course of oral prednisone to calm the immune system's overreaction. These treatments are often much more effective than OTC options for moderate to severe cases.

When is Poison Ivy a Medical Emergency?

In rare cases, a poison ivy encounter can lead to a life-threatening allergic reaction known as anaphylaxis, or systemic complications from inhaling smoke if the plant is burned. Call 911 or go to the nearest Emergency Room immediately if you experience:
  1. Difficulty breathing or swallowing.
  2. Swelling of the tongue or throat.
  3. Swelling of the eyelids to the point that they are shut.
  4. A fever over 100°F.
  5. Severe swelling in the area of the rash.
If you have inhaled smoke from burning brush that contains poison ivy, the urushiol can irritate your lungs, causing severe respiratory distress. This is a medical emergency.

When You Touch Poison Ivy, Immediate Action Can Make a Difference

If you notice a rash, intense itching, swelling, or blisters after coming into contact with poison ivy, don’t wait; take action right away. At the ER of Lufkin, our team can evaluate the severity of your reaction, provide relief for symptoms, and help you understand when to seek medical attention for a more serious response. Visit the ER of Lufkin now for fast relief and expert care. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Is poison ivy contagious from person to person? 

No. The rash itself is an allergic reaction to the oil (urushiol). You can only get the rash if you come into direct contact with the oil. 

How long does a poison ivy rash last? 

Most cases clear up within 7 to 21 days. However, in people with severe allergies, the rash can persist for 30 days or longer without medical treatment.

Should I cover the rash with a bandage? 

It is generally best to leave the rash open to the air to help it dry out. However, if the blisters are oozing, you can apply a light bandage or gauze to absorb the fluid and prevent you from scratching.

Can I get poison ivy from my dog? 

Yes. While dogs usually aren't sensitive to urushiol because of their fur, the oil can stick to their coat. 

What is the best soap to use after exposure? 

Any soap is better than none, but degreasing soaps (like those used for dishes) are particularly effective at breaking down the oils.

Does bleach cure poison ivy? 

No. You should never apply bleach to your skin. It is a harsh chemical that can cause chemical burns and further irritate an already damaged skin barrier. 

Can I get poison ivy in the winter? 

Yes. Urushiol is present in the roots and stems of the plant even when the leaves are gone. You can still get a rash by handling dormant vines or roots while gardening in the winter.

title.raw: What to Do for an Insect Sting: A Guide to Bees, Wasps, and Fire Ants
title.rendered: What to Do for an Insect Sting: A Guide to Bees, Wasps, and Fire Ants

content.raw:
Whether you were gardening, enjoying a backyard barbecue, or hiking through the Piney Woods of East Texas, an unexpected insect sting can turn a beautiful afternoon into a moment of panic. The sharp prick of a bee, the repeated stabs of a wasp, or the fiery burn of a fire ant mound are experiences most of us know all too well. While most stings result in little more than a few hours of discomfort, for some, they can be life-threatening. Understanding how to react quickly and knowing when your "normal" reaction has crossed the line into a medical emergency is essential for your peace of mind and your safety. This guide will walk you through the immediate steps to take, how to manage the pain, and when it’s time to seek professional medical help.

Recognizing the Sting: Is it a Bee, Wasp, or Fire Ant?

Different insects leave behind different "calling cards." Identifying what stung you can help you predict how your body might react and how to treat the site.

Honeybees and Bumblebees

Honeybees are unique because they are generally "one and done." According to Medline, their stinger is barbed, meaning it gets stuck in your skin and pulls away from the bee’s body, which unfortunately kills the bee but leaves the venom sac behind to continue pumping toxin into your skin.

Wasps, Hornets, and Yellow Jackets

According to the CDC, unlike bees, wasps and hornets have smooth stingers. This allows them to sting multiple times in a single encounter. Their venom is chemically different from bee venom, which is why some people may be allergic to one but not the other.

The Infamous East Texas Fire Ant

If you live in East Texas, you know that fire ants don't just bite, they sting. A fire ant will latch onto your skin with its mandibles (jaws) and then pivot its body to sting you multiple times in a circular pattern. According to the CDC, fire ant venom causes a distinct burning sensation, followed by the formation of a small, white pustule (blister) within 24 hours.

Immediate First Aid: Steps to Take Right Away

The moments immediately following a sting are the most important for limiting the amount of venom that enters your system.

How to Safely Remove a Stinger

If you were stung by a honeybee, you need to get the stinger out fast. Research from the NIH suggests that the method of removal is less important than the speed. Use your fingernail, a piece of gauze, or the edge of a credit card to scrape the stinger out. Avoid using tweezers to "squeeze" the stinger, as this can inadvertently compress the venom sac and inject more toxin into your wound.

Cleaning and Protecting the Site

Once the stinger is out (or if there wasn't one to begin with), follow these steps:
  1. Wash the area: Use mild soap and water to prevent secondary infection.
  2. Disinfect: Use an antiseptic if available.
  3. Elevate: If you were stung on an arm or leg, keeping the limb elevated can help reduce the initial rush of swelling.

Managing Pain and Swelling at Home

For most people, a sting results in "local" symptoms: redness, itching, and swelling at the site of the sting.

Home Remedies vs. Over-the-Counter Options

To manage a standard reaction, the following is recommended:
  • Ice Packs: Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth for 10–20 minutes at a time. This constricts blood vessels and slows the spread of venom while numbing the pain.
  • Oral Antihistamines: Over-the-counter medications like diphenhydramine (Benadryl) or cetirizine (Zyrtec) can help reduce itching and hives.
  • Hydrocortisone Cream: A 1% hydrocortisone cream applied to the site can soothe the skin and reduce redness.
  • Pain Relief: Acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help manage the "throbbing" sensation often associated with wasp stings.
A Note on Fire Ants: Whatever you do, do not pop the blisters. Fire ant pustules are sterile, but breaking them open creates an entry point for bacteria, which can lead to a serious skin infection like cellulitis.

When to Worry: Normal Reactions vs. Allergic Reactions

It is normal for a sting to hurt and swell. In fact, a "Large Local Reaction" can involve swelling that extends beyond the sting site (for example, a sting on the forearm causing the whole arm to swell). While alarming, this is generally not life-threatening.

Signs of Anaphylaxis (Systemic Reaction)

Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction that requires immediate emergency care. You should call 911 or head to the nearest emergency room if you experience:
  • Difficulty breathing or wheezing.
  • Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat.
  • A rapid or weak pulse.
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting.
  • Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
  • A widespread skin rash or hives away from the sting site.
If you have a known allergy and carry an Epinephrine Auto-Injector (EpiPen), use it immediately at the first sign of a systemic reaction and seek professional medical evaluation afterward, as "rebound" reactions can occur.

Why You Should Visit Urgent Care for an Insect Sting

While minor stings can be handled at home, there are several reasons to visit an urgent care center or ER:
  1. Multiple Stings: If you have been swarmed by fire ants or disturbed a wasp nest and received dozens of stings, the sheer volume of venom can be toxic even if you aren't allergic.
  2. Stings in Sensitive Areas: A sting inside the mouth or throat can cause swelling that blocks the airway.
  3. Signs of Infection: If the redness starts spreading after 24–48 hours, or if you develop a fever or yellow drainage from the site, you may need antibiotics.
  4. Tetanus Concerns: If it has been more than 5–10 years since your last tetanus shot, a puncture wound from a stinger is a good reason to get a booster.

Bee, Wasp, or Fire Ant Sting: Quick Relief + When to Get Checked

Not sure if it’s "normal" swelling or something more? If you have trouble breathing, facial/throat swelling, widespread hives, or you were stung many times, come to the ER of Lufkin for immediate evaluation and treatment. Visit the ER of Lufkin now for fast relief and expert care. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates

FAQs

How long does a bee sting usually last?

Most pain subsides within a few hours, but swelling and redness can peak at 48 hours and may last up to a week. If symptoms worsen after two days, consult a healthcare provider.

Is it true that baking soda helps with insect stings?

A paste of baking soda and water is a common home remedy that may help neutralize the acidity of some venoms and reduce itching, though it is not a substitute for medical treatment in severe cases.

Can you develop a bee allergy later in life?

Yes. You can develop an allergy to stinging insects at any time, even if you have been stung before without a problem.

What does an infected insect sting look like?

An infected sting may feel warm to the touch, have red streaks radiating from the site, or produce pus. Fever and chills are also signs that the infection has become more serious.

How do I stop fire ants from itching?

Avoid scratching, which can break the skin. Use topical steroid creams and oral antihistamines as recommended by a doctor.

Do I need a doctor if I’m not having an allergic reaction?

You should see a doctor if the sting is in your eye, mouth, or if you have received an unusually high number of stings at once.

title.raw: Signs of Severe Dehydration: When It’s Time for Professional Care
title.rendered: Signs of Severe Dehydration: When It’s Time for Professional Care

content.raw:
We’ve all been there: a busy afternoon where you realize you haven’t reached for your water bottle in hours, or a bout of stomach flu that leaves you feeling drained. Usually, a few tall glasses of water or an electrolyte drink do the trick. But sometimes, dehydration isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a medical emergency. Understanding the signs of severe dehydration is about more than just knowing when to drink water; it’s about knowing when your body can no longer fix the problem on its own. When your system loses more fluid than it takes in, your organs, muscles, and brain begin to struggle. At a certain point, oral rehydration isn't fast enough, and medical intervention like IV fluids becomes necessary to prevent serious complications.

What is Dehydration?

At its simplest, dehydration occurs when your body doesn’t have enough water and electrolytes to carry out its normal functions. According to MedlinePlus, water makes up about two-thirds of a healthy body. It lubricates joints, aids digestion, flushes out waste, and keeps your skin healthy. When you lose too much fluid, whether through sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, or increased urination, you also lose essential salts like sodium and potassium. These minerals are vital for your heart to beat and your brain to send signals.

Recognizing the Progression: Mild vs. Moderate

Before we dive into the "danger zone," it’s helpful to know how dehydration typically starts. Most people experience mild to moderate dehydration first.
  • Mild Dehydration: You might feel a bit thirsty, have a slightly dry mouth, or notice your urine is a darker yellow than usual.
  • Moderate Dehydration: You may start to feel fatigued, experience a headache, or notice that you are urinating less frequently.
While these stages can usually be treated at home by sipping fluids, they are the warning shots your body fires before things take a turn for the worse.

Signs of Severe Dehydration: When It Becomes an Emergency

Severe dehydration is a life-threatening condition. At this stage, your blood volume can actually drop, leading to a dangerous fall in blood pressure. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), once you reach this level, your body enters a state of crisis.

1. Mental Status and Neurological Changes

One of the most telling signs of severe dehydration is how it affects your brain. If a loved one seems suddenly confused, irritable, or unusually sleepy, their brain may not be receiving enough blood flow. In extreme cases, this can lead to delirium or unconsciousness.

2. Physical Indicators: Skin Turgor and Sunken Eyes

Doctors often check "skin turgor" to assess hydration levels. If you pinch the skin on the back of your hand and it stays in a "tent" shape rather than snapping back instantly, you are likely severely dehydrated. Additionally, eyes may appear sunken or dull, and the mouth and mucous membranes will feel completely parched, lacking any saliva.

3. The "Red Alert" Symptoms in Adults

If you or someone you are caring for experiences the following, seek emergency care immediately:
  • Extreme Thirst: A desperate, unquenchable need for water.
  • Lack of Urination: Passing no urine for 8 hours or more, or urine that is extremely dark (like the color of tea or amber).
  • Rapid Heartbeat and Breathing: Your heart pumps faster to compensate for low blood volume.
  • Dizziness or Fainting: Feeling lightheaded when you try to stand up.
  • Low Blood Pressure: A sign that the circulatory system is struggling.

Dehydration in Vulnerable Groups

While anyone can become dehydrated, infants and senior citizens are at the highest risk. Their bodies don't manage fluid balance quite as efficiently as younger adults.

Specific Warning Signs for Babies

Infants can become severely dehydrated very quickly, especially if they have a fever or diarrhea. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends watching for:
  • A sunken soft spot (fontanelle) on the top of the head.
  • No wet diapers for three hours or more.
  • Crying without producing any tears.
  • Unusual sleepiness or fussiness.

How Aging Masks Thirst

For older adults, the "thirst mechanism" becomes less sensitive with age. You might be dehydrated without even feeling thirsty. Seniors are also more likely to be on medications, like diuretics for blood pressure, which can increase fluid loss. Caregivers need to monitor fluid intake even if the patient says they aren't thirsty.

Why Water Isn't Always Enough: The Need for IV Fluids

You might wonder: If I’m dehydrated, why can’t I just drink a lot of water? In severe cases, the body reaches a "point of no return" for oral intake. If a patient is vomiting uncontrollably, they cannot keep fluids down. If they are confused or unconscious, they cannot safely swallow. This is where Intravenous (IV) rehydration comes in. By bypassing the digestive system, medical professionals can pump a precise balance of water and electrolytes, usually a saline or Ringer’s lactate solution, directly into the bloodstream.

Benefits of IV Fluids include:

  • Immediate Absorption: The fluids begin working the second they enter the vein.
  • Electrolyte Balance: Doctors can tailor the IV bag to include specific minerals the patient is missing.
  • Organ Protection: Rapid rehydration helps prevent kidney failure and shock.

When to Head to Urgent Care or the ER

If you are experiencing mild symptoms, an urgent care center is a great place to receive a quick IV treatment and get back on your feet. However, if symptoms include fainting, chest pain, or complete confusion, the Emergency Room is the safest choice. The CDC notes that staying hydrated is a daily task, but when illness strikes, the window between "feeling off" and "medical emergency" can be surprisingly small.

Prevention: Staying Ahead of the Thirst

The best way to treat severe dehydration is to never let it reach that point.
  • Drink consistently: Don't wait until you're thirsty to drink.
  • Monitor your urine: Aim for a pale straw color.
  • Eat hydrating foods: Watermelon, cucumbers, and oranges are great sources of fluid.
  • Adjust for activity: If you are sweating heavily or it’s a humid day, increase your intake significantly. In extreme heat, learn to tell heat exhaustion from heat stroke before you need to.

Staying Hydrated for World Cup 2026 in the Texas Heat

Between long drives to the stadiums and all-day gatherings in the summer sun, the FIFA World Cup 2026 will have fans pushing through the hottest stretch of a Texas summer. With matches in Houston and the Dallas–Arlington area, Lufkin sits right between the two host regions, so whether you're driving to a game or hosting a watch party in the backyard, here's what to keep in mind to stay ahead of the heat.

How much should I drink during an all-day watch party or tailgate?

More than you'd think, and earlier than you'd think. The CDC recommends drinking plenty of fluids and not waiting until you feel thirsty, since thirst tends to lag what your body has already lost. Keep water with you, and take regular breaks in the shade rather than relying on finding a drink later.

I'm driving from Houston to Dallas for a match. How do I stay hydrated on the road?

A long summer drive, a warm car, and a packed schedule make it easy to skip fluids. The CDC travel-health guidance notes that the more active you are in high heat, the more likely you are to develop a heat-related illness, so pack a refillable bottle, sip steadily, and build in stops. If you're passing through Lufkin and feeling wiped out, care is right on your route.

Does beer at the watch party dehydrate me faster?

It can. The CDC points out that alcoholic and very sugary drinks actually cause your body to lose more fluid, so they work against you on a hot day. Alternating each one with a glass of water helps you enjoy the match and stay ahead of it.

What early signs should I watch for at an outdoor event?

MedlinePlus lists early signs such as thirst, a dry or sticky mouth, urinating less, darker yellow urine, headache, and muscle cramps. Those are your body's cues to get into the shade, cool down, and rehydrate before things progress further.

When is it time to get professional help?

If steady sipping isn't turning things around, it's worth getting checked. For more significant fluid loss, replacing fluids and electrolytes through an IV is a common treatment and can restore hydration quickly. Our team provides dehydration treatment in Lufkin around the clock, with on-site labs and IV fluids, so traveling fans and local families can get back on their feet.

If you’re seeing red-flag dehydration symptoms like no urination for 8+ hours, dark "tea-colored" urine, fainting, rapid heartbeat, severe weakness, or confusion, don’t wait for it to "pass." ER of Lufkin can evaluate what’s going on and provide medical-grade rehydration (including IV fluids when appropriate) to help protect your kidneys, heart, and overall stability. FAQs

How long does it take to recover from severe dehydration with an IV?

Most patients begin to feel significantly better within 30 to 60 minutes of starting IV fluids. However, full cellular recovery and electrolyte balancing may take several hours or even a day of monitoring, depending on the severity.

Can I get an IV for dehydration at an urgent care?

Yes, most urgent care centers are equipped to provide IV rehydration therapy for moderate to severe dehydration, provided the patient is stable and not showing signs of shock.

What color is urine when you are severely dehydrated?

Severely dehydrated urine is typically a dark amber or "burnt orange" color. If it looks like tea or cola, this is a sign of extreme dehydration and potential kidney distress.

Can dehydration cause a fever?

While dehydration itself doesn't usually cause a high fever, it can cause your body temperature to rise because you can't sweat enough to cool down. Conversely, a fever caused by an infection often leads to dehydration.

Is Gatorade as good as an IV?

For mild dehydration, sports drinks or oral rehydration salts are excellent. However, they are absorbed slowly through the gut. In severe cases, especially with vomiting, an IV is much more effective and faster.

Can dehydration cause heart palpitations?

Yes. When blood volume is low, your heart has to beat faster and harder to move oxygen through your body, which can feel like a racing or fluttering heart.

title.raw: When Is an Allergic Reaction an Emergency? (Understanding Anaphylaxis)
title.rendered: When Is an Allergic Reaction an Emergency? (Understanding Anaphylaxis)

content.raw:
We’ve all been there: a scratchy throat after a picnic, a few itchy hives after trying a new laundry detergent, or a runny nose during hay fever season. Most of the time, allergies are an inconvenience we manage with an over-the-counter antihistamine. However, for millions of people, an allergy isn't just a seasonal annoyance; it's a hidden landmine. When the body’s immune system overreacts to a trigger, it can trigger anaphylaxis, a rapid and potentially fatal allergic reaction. In these moments, your ability to distinguish between a "wait and see" situation and a medical emergency is the most important tool you have.

What Exactly is Anaphylaxis?

According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), anaphylaxis is a severe, systemic allergic reaction that affects the entire body. Think of your immune system as a security team. In a normal allergy, the team overreacts to a "trespasser" (like pollen) by causing a runny nose. In anaphylaxis, the security team panics, shuts down the building’s power, and locks all the doors. This "panic" causes your immune system to release a flood of chemicals that can cause you to go into shock. Your blood pressure drops suddenly, and your airways narrow, blocking your ability to breathe.

Is It Just an Allergy or an Emergency?

One of the most common questions we hear at the clinic is, "How do I know if this is serious?" The Medline notes that while mild symptoms are uncomfortable, they don't usually involve the respiratory or circulatory systems.
Mild/Moderate Reaction (Non-Emergency) Severe Reaction (Anaphylaxis - Call 911)
Itchy or runny nose Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat
A few isolated hives Shortness of breath or wheezing
Watery, itchy eyes Sudden drop in blood pressure (feeling faint)
Mild stomach upset Rapid or weak pulse
Localized swelling at a sting site Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea

The "Red Flag" Symptoms: When to Call 911

If you or a loved one experiences the following "Red Flag" symptoms, do not wait. According to the Medline, anaphylaxis can occur within seconds or minutes of exposure.

1. Respiratory Distress

This is often the first sign of danger. It may feel like your throat is "closing up." You might hear a high-pitched sound when breathing (stridor) or experience repetitive coughing and gasping for air.

2. Cardiovascular Collapse (Shock)

When the body goes into anaphylactic shock, blood vessels dilate rapidly. This causes blood pressure to plummet. The person may become extremely pale, feel dizzy, or lose consciousness. This is a sign that the heart is struggling to pump blood to vital organs.

3. Skin and Gastrointestinal Warnings

While hives are common, in a severe reaction, they often spread across the entire body. This may be accompanied by swelling (angioedema) around the eyes and lips. Interestingly, sudden, severe vomiting or cramping after an insect sting or a meal can also be a primary sign of anaphylaxis.

Common Triggers for Severe Reactions

While you can be allergic to almost anything, the FDA identifies specific high-risk triggers that are most likely to cause anaphylaxis:
  • Foods: Peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, milk, and eggs. Our guide to recognizing severe food allergic reactions covers what to watch for after trying new foods.
  • Stings: Bees, wasps, hornets, and fire ants.
  • Medications: Certain antibiotics (like penicillin) or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
  • Latex: Often found in medical gloves or balloons.

The Biphasic Reaction: Why You Can’t Relax Too Soon

One of the most dangerous aspects of a severe allergic reaction is the biphasic reaction. As documented by MedlinePlus, this is a "second wave" of symptoms. You might treat the first reaction with epinephrine, feel much better, and think you’re in the clear only for a second, more severe reaction occurs 2 to 24 hours later. This is why every person who uses an EpiPen or experiences anaphylaxis must be observed in an Emergency Room for several hours.

Immediate Action Steps: What to Do

If you suspect someone is having a severe allergic reaction:
  1. Call 911 Immediately. Do not attempt to drive the person to the hospital yourself if they are struggling to breathe.
  2. Use an Epinephrine Auto-Injector (EpiPen). If the person has an auto-injector, use it in the outer thigh. Do not hesitate; the risk of the reaction is far greater than the risk of the medication.
  3. Positioning. Lay the person flat on their back. If they are vomiting, turn them on their side. If they are struggling to breathe, they may need to sit up, but keep their legs elevated if possible to help with blood pressure.
  4. Stay Calm. Reassure the patient. Stress can increase the heart rate and worsen the perception of respiratory distress.

Don’t Wait for Severe Allergy Symptoms

When allergies turn serious, minutes matter. If you or a loved one has trouble breathing, swelling of the lips/tongue/throat, wheezing, faintness, or severe vomiting after a food, sting, or medication exposure, don’t “wait it out.” ER of Lufkin is here 24/7. Come in right away for evaluation and monitoring, especially after using an EpiPen, because symptoms can return hours later. Visit the ER of Lufkin now for fast relief and expert care. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Can Benadryl stop anaphylaxis?

No. While antihistamines like Benadryl can help with itching or hives, they cannot stop the life-threatening throat swelling or low blood pressure associated with anaphylaxis. 

How fast does anaphylaxis happen?

Symptoms usually start within 5 to 30 minutes of contact with an allergen, but they can sometimes take up to an hour to appear.

What if I’m not sure it’s anaphylaxis? Should I still use the EpiPen?

Yes. Medical experts agree that it is safer to use epinephrine if you suspect a severe reaction than to wait.

Can you have anaphylaxis without hives?

Yes. In about 10% to 20% of cases, patients do not develop any skin symptoms. They may only experience respiratory distress or a sudden drop in blood pressure.

Do I still need to go to the ER if the EpiPen worked?

Yes, absolutely. Because of the risk of a "biphasic" (second) reaction, you must be monitored by medical professionals for at least 4 to 6 hours.

Visit the ER of Lufkin now for fast relief and expert care.

Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313

Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Can Benadryl stop anaphylaxis?

No. While antihistamines like Benadryl can help with itching or hives, they cannot stop the life-threatening throat swelling or low blood pressure associated with anaphylaxis. 

How fast does anaphylaxis happen?

Symptoms usually start within 5 to 30 minutes of contact with an allergen, but they can sometimes take up to an hour to appear.

What if I’m not sure it’s anaphylaxis? Should I still use the EpiPen?

Yes. Medical experts agree that it is safer to use epinephrine if you suspect a severe reaction than to wait.

Can you have anaphylaxis without hives?

Yes. In about 10% to 20% of cases, patients do not develop any skin symptoms. They may only experience respiratory distress or a sudden drop in blood pressure.

Yes, absolutely. Because of the risk of a “biphasic” (second) reaction, you must be monitored by medical professionals for at least 4 to 6 hours.

title.raw: Understanding Blood Pressure: Numbers, Stages, and How to Manage High BP
title.rendered: Understanding Blood Pressure: Numbers, Stages, and How to Manage High BP

content.raw:
Blood pressure is one of the most useful signals of your overall health, but it is often misunderstood. Per the CDC, nearly half of US adults have high blood pressure (hypertension), but only about 1 in 4 have it under control.

Most people with high blood pressure feel completely fine, which is why it has earned the nickname "the silent killer." This guide explains what your numbers mean, the four blood pressure stages, how to take an accurate reading at home, and how to lower your numbers through lifestyle and medication.

If your reading hits 180/120 mm Hg or higher, especially with chest pain, vision change, weakness, or a severe headache, that is a medical emergency. See our hypertension crisis guide or call 911.

What Do Your Blood Pressure Numbers Actually Mean?

When a nurse wraps that cuff around your arm, they are measuring the force of your blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. The reading is two numbers, written like a fraction (for example, 120/80).

Systolic (Top Number)

This measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats. It tells your doctor how hard your heart is working to push blood out.

Diastolic (Bottom Number)

This measures the pressure when your heart is at rest between beats. It reflects the resistance in your arteries while the heart refills.

Why Both Numbers Matter

Per the NHLBI, if either number stays high over time, it damages blood vessels. The systolic number is a stronger predictor of heart attack and stroke risk for adults over 50. The diastolic number tends to matter more for adults under 50.

Pulse pressure (top number minus bottom number) is also useful. A wide pulse pressure (over 60 mm Hg) can signal stiffer arteries and higher cardiovascular risk.

Blood Pressure Categories: Normal, Elevated, Stage 1, Stage 2

Per the American Heart Association and CDC, blood pressure falls into five categories.

CategorySystolic (top)Diastolic (bottom)What to Do
NormalUnder 120Under 80Recheck yearly. Maintain healthy lifestyle.
Elevated120 to 129Under 80Lifestyle changes. Monitor at home.
Stage 1 Hypertension130 to 139OR 80 to 89Lifestyle changes. Medication if other heart-disease risk factors.
Stage 2 Hypertension140 or higherOR 90 or higherLifestyle changes plus one or two medications. See your doctor.
Hypertensive Crisis180 or higherAND/OR 120 or higherRecheck after 5 minutes. If still high with symptoms, call 911. See hypertension crisis guide.

The categories are based on an average of two or more readings on at least two different days. A single high reading does not automatically put you in a higher category.

Stage 1 vs Stage 2 Hypertension: What These Numbers Mean for Your Health

Stage 1 Hypertension (130 to 139 / 80 to 89)

Per the AHA, Stage 1 doubles your risk of cardiovascular disease compared to normal BP. Most patients without other risk factors start with lifestyle changes alone for 3 to 6 months.

Medication is added if you also have diabetes, kidney disease, prior heart attack, or a 10-year cardiovascular risk score above 10%. Many people can keep Stage 1 BP under control with diet, exercise, and weight loss alone.

Stage 2 Hypertension (140+ / 90+)

Stage 2 usually requires medication from the start, plus lifestyle changes. Per the NHLBI, doctors often prescribe two medications at once for Stage 2 because one drug rarely brings BP into the normal range.

Untreated Stage 2 hypertension shortens life expectancy by 5 to 10 years on average and significantly raises stroke, heart attack, and kidney failure risk.

How to Take an Accurate Blood Pressure Reading at Home

Home readings are often more accurate than office readings because they avoid white coat syndrome (BP spikes at the doctor's office from anxiety). Per the AHA, follow these steps for a reliable reading.

Before You Measure

  • Avoid caffeine, exercise, and smoking for 30 minutes
  • Empty your bladder
  • Sit quietly for 5 minutes before the reading
  • Use a validated upper-arm cuff (wrist cuffs are less reliable)

During the Reading

  • Sit with your back supported and feet flat on the floor
  • Rest your arm on a flat surface at heart level
  • Wrap the cuff on bare skin, not over a sleeve
  • Do not talk, eat, or use a phone
  • Take two readings 1 to 2 minutes apart, at the same time each day

White Coat Syndrome and Masked Hypertension

White coat syndrome is when BP reads higher at the doctor's office than at home, due to anxiety. Masked hypertension is the opposite: normal at the office but high at home.

Both are real and both raise cardiovascular risk. If your home and office readings differ by more than 10 mm Hg, ask your doctor about a 24-hour ambulatory BP monitor for a more accurate picture.

Why Untreated High Blood Pressure Damages Your Body Over Time

Most people with high blood pressure have no symptoms until damage is already done. That is why daily monitoring matters more than waiting for warning signs.

The damage builds slowly over months and years. Per the FDA, untreated hypertension is a leading cause of heart attacks, strokes, and kidney failure.

What High BP Does Over Years

  • Arteries. Constant pressure creates micro-tears. Your body repairs them with scar tissue, which traps cholesterol and leads to atherosclerosis (clogged arteries)
  • Heart. The heart muscle thickens to push against the higher pressure, eventually weakening (heart failure)
  • Kidneys. The small blood vessels in the kidneys get damaged, slowly cutting filtering capacity
  • Brain. Damaged vessels raise risk of stroke, vascular dementia, and cognitive decline
  • Eyes. The tiny vessels in the retina can leak or bleed (hypertensive retinopathy)
  • Sexual function. Reduced blood flow can cause erectile dysfunction in men and lower libido in women

The good news: most of this damage slows or stops once BP is brought under control, even if it took years to develop.

How to Lower Your Blood Pressure with Lifestyle Changes

The strongest tool for lowering BP is consistent daily habits. Per the CDC and AHA, these changes have the best evidence.

Follow the DASH Eating Plan

The DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) can lower systolic BP by about 11 mm Hg. It focuses on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean protein, low-fat dairy, and nuts. It limits red meat, sugary drinks, and packaged snacks.

Cut Sodium

Aim for under 2,300 mg of sodium per day. Under 1,500 mg per day is even better and can lower BP by another 5 to 6 mm Hg. Most sodium comes from packaged foods and restaurant meals, not the salt shaker.

Move More

Get at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week (brisk walking, swimming, cycling). Even 30 minutes of walking five days a week can lower systolic BP by 5 to 8 mm Hg.

Lose Weight If You Need To

Every 2 pounds of weight loss can lower BP by about 1 mm Hg. Losing 10 to 20 pounds can move someone from Stage 2 into Stage 1, or from Stage 1 into Elevated.

Limit Alcohol and Quit Tobacco

Limit alcohol to one drink a day for women, two for men. Quit tobacco, including vaping. Treat sleep apnea if you have it, since untreated apnea drives BP up overnight.

Medications for High Blood Pressure: What Your Doctor May Prescribe

If lifestyle changes alone do not bring your BP into the goal range, your doctor will add medication. Per the NHLBI, several drug classes work, and combinations are common.

  • Thiazide diuretics (water pills): help your body shed excess sodium and water. Often the first drug for newly diagnosed Stage 1 or 2.
  • ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril): relax blood vessels by blocking a hormone that narrows them. Common side effect: dry cough.
  • ARBs (losartan, valsartan): similar to ACE inhibitors but without the cough. Often used when ACE inhibitors are not tolerated.
  • Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, diltiazem): relax blood vessel walls. Common side effects include leg swelling and constipation.
  • Beta blockers (metoprolol, atenolol): slow the heart rate and reduce the force of each beat. Typically added when other classes are not enough or for patients with certain heart conditions.

If you are prescribed medication, take it exactly as ordered. Stopping a BP medication abruptly can cause a rebound spike. Talk to your doctor about side effects rather than stopping on your own.

When to See Your Doctor About High Blood Pressure (Not the ER)

Most blood pressure concerns are handled by your primary care doctor or a cardiologist, not the ER. Schedule a same-week appointment if any of these apply:

  • Home readings are consistently over 130/80 over two weeks
  • You feel side effects from a BP medication (dizziness, dry cough, swelling)
  • Your BP is not improving on your current treatment
  • You are planning a pregnancy and take antihypertensives
  • You have new chest discomfort with activity that goes away with rest (possible stable angina)
  • You feel a fluttering or skipped heartbeat (possible atrial fibrillation)

For 180/120 with symptoms (chest pain, vision change, weakness, slurred speech, severe headache), do not wait for a doctor visit. That is a hypertensive emergency. Call 911 or go to the ER. See our hypertension crisis guide for full emergency signs.

Get Cardiac Care at ER of Lufkin

For ongoing blood pressure management, your primary care doctor or cardiologist is the right starting point. ER of Lufkin is here for cardiac emergencies: hypertensive crisis with symptoms, chest pain that may be a heart attack, sudden weakness or vision change suggesting a stroke, or a fast or irregular heartbeat with dizziness.

Phone: (936) 427-1313
Open 24 hours, 7 days a week
info@eroflufkin.com

FAQs

What is the difference between Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension?

Stage 1 is 130 to 139 systolic OR 80 to 89 diastolic. Stage 2 is 140 or higher OR 90 or higher.

Stage 1 is often managed with lifestyle changes alone for 3 to 6 months. Stage 2 usually needs medication from the start, often two drugs at once.

How accurate are home blood pressure monitors?

Validated upper-arm cuffs are very accurate when used correctly. Wrist cuffs are less reliable. Per the AHA, bring your home monitor to your next doctor visit so they can compare it to their office reading and confirm it is accurate.

Can I lower my blood pressure without medication?

Often yes, especially for Elevated and Stage 1. The DASH diet, sodium reduction, weight loss, and 150 minutes of weekly exercise can lower systolic BP by 15 to 25 mm Hg combined.

For Stage 2, lifestyle changes are still important but usually need to be paired with medication.

What should my blood pressure be by age?

Per the AHA, the goal is under 120/80 for most adults. The targets do not change much with age, although doctors may accept slightly higher numbers in older adults to avoid dizziness and falls from BP medications.

Why does my blood pressure read differently at the doctor's office?

That is white coat syndrome: anxiety raises BP at the office. Home readings are often more accurate.

If your home and office readings differ by more than 10 mm Hg, ask about a 24-hour ambulatory BP monitor.

How long does it take for lifestyle changes to lower BP?

You can see a measurable drop within 2 to 4 weeks of starting the DASH diet, cutting sodium, and exercising regularly. Bigger gains come over 3 to 6 months as weight loss and fitness build.

Does ER of Lufkin treat blood pressure emergencies?

Yes. Our 24-hour emergency room handles hypertensive crisis (180/120 or higher with symptoms) with IV antihypertensive medications, continuous monitoring, EKG, and ICU admission if needed. For full emergency signs, see our hypertension crisis guide. For ongoing BP management, see your primary care doctor or cardiologist.

title.raw: When is Dizziness or Vertigo an Emergency?
title.rendered: When is Dizziness or Vertigo an Emergency?

content.raw:
Dizziness and vertigo are sensations that most people experience at some point in their lives, but they can also be signs of something much more serious. If you’re feeling dizzy or experiencing vertigo, you may wonder if it’s a simple issue like dehydration or something that requires emergency medical attention. Knowing the difference is essential for your health and safety. In this blog, we’ll explore what dizziness and vertigo are, their common causes, and most importantly, when these symptoms become an emergency. By the end, you’ll understand how to respond to these symptoms and why it’s crucial to seek immediate medical care if needed.

What Are Dizziness and Vertigo?

Defining Dizziness

Dizziness is a broad term that describes a range of sensations, from lightheadedness to unsteadiness. It often occurs when there’s a sudden drop in blood pressure, dehydration, or sudden movements. It’s usually not a cause for concern and can be remedied with a little rest, water, or a change in position.

Understanding Vertigo

Vertigo, on the other hand, is a specific type of dizziness where individuals feel like they or their surroundings are spinning. Unlike regular dizziness, vertigo can be a symptom of inner ear problems, vestibular disorders, or even neurological conditions. It’s important to differentiate between the two, as vertigo can indicate a more serious health condition.

Common Causes of Dizziness and Vertigo

Causes of Dizziness

  • Mild Dehydration: Not drinking enough fluids can lead to a drop in blood pressure, causing dizziness.
  • Stress and Anxiety: High levels of anxiety can cause a feeling of dizziness or lightheadedness.
  • Low Blood Pressure: Standing up too quickly can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure, making you feel dizzy.
  • Medication Side Effects: Certain medications, especially those for blood pressure or anxiety, can cause dizziness as a side effect.
  • Inner Ear Infections: Labyrinthitis, an infection of the inner ear, can cause dizziness due to its role in balance regulation.

More Serious Causes of Dizziness

  • Stroke or Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA): According to the CDC, dizziness can sometimes be a sign of a stroke or TIA, especially when accompanied by other symptoms like slurred speech or numbness.
  • Meniere’s Disease: According to MedlinePlus, this condition, affecting the inner ear, can cause recurrent dizziness and vertigo along with hearing loss. (More information on Meniere's disease can be found on).
  • Vestibular Neuritis: According to NIH, inflammation of the vestibular nerve, which controls balance, can cause vertigo and dizziness.
  • Heart Problems: Arrhythmias or low blood flow to the brain can lead to dizziness or vertigo, often accompanied by chest pain or shortness of breath.

When Should Dizziness or Vertigo Be Considered an Emergency?

Key Red Flags for Emergency Care

Certain symptoms accompanying dizziness or vertigo warrant immediate medical attention. If you or a loved one experiences any of the following, don’t wait – seek emergency care immediately:
  • Severe or Sudden Vertigo: When vertigo is sudden and severe, especially if accompanied by nausea or vomiting.
  • Slurred Speech or Difficulty Understanding Speech: This could be a sign of a stroke.
  • Weakness or Numbness on One Side of the Body: This may indicate a stroke or TIA.
  • Sudden Loss of Vision: Losing vision in one or both eyes, especially with dizziness, is a red flag for serious conditions like stroke.
  • Severe Headache: A headache that doesn’t go away or is different from previous ones can signal a neurological emergency.
  • Difficulty Walking or Maintaining Balance: If the dizziness causes you to fall or have trouble staying steady, it’s important to seek medical help.

The Connection Between Stroke and Dizziness

Dizziness is a key symptom of a stroke, and recognizing this early can be life-saving. If dizziness is accompanied by other symptoms, such as weakness, slurred speech, or confusion, it’s important to treat it as a stroke until proven otherwise. Time is critical in stroke treatment; the quicker the intervention, the better the chances of recovery.

Diagnostic Tests and Treatment for Dizziness and Vertigo

How Healthcare Providers Diagnose the Cause of Dizziness

A healthcare provider will usually start by performing a physical and neurological exam to assess balance, coordination, and reflexes. Common diagnostic tools for dizziness include:
  • Balance Tests: These assess how well your inner ear, brain, and eyes work together.
  • Imaging: MRI or CT scans may be used to rule out serious conditions like strokes or tumors.
  • Blood Pressure Monitoring: Checking for sudden drops in blood pressure when standing up.
  • Heart Monitoring: If heart-related issues are suspected, an ECG or Holter monitor may be used.

Common Treatments for Dizziness and Vertigo

Treatment for dizziness or vertigo depends on the underlying cause:
  • Medications: Anti-nausea and anti-dizziness medications can help alleviate symptoms.
  • Vestibular Rehabilitation: Physical therapy exercises designed to help you regain balance and coordination.
  • Surgical Options: In cases like Meniere’s disease, surgery may be necessary to manage symptoms.

How to Manage and Prevent Dizziness and Vertigo at Home

Lifestyle Adjustments for Dizziness Prevention

  • Stay Hydrated: Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day to prevent dehydration.
  • Manage Stress: Engage in relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or meditation.
  • Eat Regularly: Skipping meals can lead to low blood sugar, which can cause dizziness.
  • Limit Alcohol and Caffeine: Both can disrupt the inner ear and lead to dizziness or vertigo.
  • Balance Exercises: Regular physical activity can help improve your balance and prevent vertigo.

Home Remedies for Mild Dizziness

For mild cases of dizziness, try:
  • Resting in a Quiet Room: Lying down in a calm space can help relieve dizziness.
  • Performing Balance Exercises: If you have benign positional vertigo, exercises like the Epley maneuver can help reposition the crystals in your inner ear and relieve symptoms.

When to Seek Professional Help

When to Call Your Doctor

If dizziness or vertigo lasts longer than a few minutes or if it worsens over time, contact your doctor. If you experience dizziness along with other symptoms like chest pain, severe headache, or weakness, seek immediate medical care.

Urgent Care vs. Emergency Care

While mild dizziness or vertigo can often be treated in a doctor’s office, if you experience more severe symptoms, it’s crucial to go to the emergency room. Quick diagnosis and treatment are vital, especially when the cause of dizziness could be life-threatening, like a stroke.

Act Fast: When Dizziness or Vertigo Becomes an Emergency

If you or a loved one is experiencing dizziness, vertigo, or any of the symptoms outlined in this blog, don’t wait; your health is too important. Contact us today to schedule a consultation with one of our specialists and get the care you need. Trust the ER of Lufkin for fast, expert care when every second counts. Whether it's a sudden onset of dizziness, vertigo, or other symptoms, we're here 24/7 to ensure you're treated like family, not just a number. Visit the ER of Lufkin now for fast relief and expert care. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What are the first signs of vertigo that could signal an emergency?

Suddenly, severe spinning sensations along with nausea, vomiting, and difficulty walking could signal an emergency.

How do I know if my dizziness is from low blood pressure or something more serious?

If dizziness occurs with fainting, nausea, or blurred vision, or lasts for an extended period, it may be time to seek professional help.

Can vertigo be a sign of a stroke?

Yes, vertigo combined with weakness, slurred speech, or numbness can indicate a stroke.

What should I do if I feel lightheaded while driving?

Pull over safely and rest. If the lightheadedness persists, seek medical attention.

Are there exercises I can do at home to stop dizziness from returning?

Yes, balance exercises like the Epley maneuver can help alleviate symptoms of benign positional vertigo.

What’s the difference between dizziness and vertigo?

Dizziness is a broad term that includes lightheadedness, while vertigo is a specific type of dizziness where you feel like you or your surroundings are spinning.

How can I reduce the risk of dizziness as I age?

Stay hydrated, eat regularly, exercise to improve balance, and manage stress.

In this blog, we’ll explore what dizziness and vertigo are, their common causes, and most importantly, when these symptoms become an emergency. By the end, you’ll understand how to respond to these symptoms and why it’s crucial to seek immediate medical care if needed.

What Are Dizziness and Vertigo?

Defining Dizziness

Dizziness is a broad term that describes a range of sensations, from lightheadedness to unsteadiness. It often occurs when there’s a sudden drop in blood pressure, dehydration, or sudden movements. It’s usually not a cause for concern and can be remedied with a little rest, water, or a change in position.

Understanding Vertigo

Vertigo, on the other hand, is a specific type of dizziness where individuals feel like they or their surroundings are spinning. Unlike regular dizziness, vertigo can be a symptom of inner ear problems, vestibular disorders, or even neurological conditions. It’s important to differentiate between the two, as vertigo can indicate a more serious health condition.

Common Causes of Dizziness and Vertigo

Causes of Dizziness

  • Mild Dehydration: Not drinking enough fluids can lead to a drop in blood pressure, causing dizziness.
  • Stress and Anxiety: High levels of anxiety can cause a feeling of dizziness or lightheadedness.
  • Low Blood Pressure: Standing up too quickly can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure, making you feel dizzy.
  • Medication Side Effects: Certain medications, especially those for blood pressure or anxiety, can cause dizziness as a side effect.
  • Inner Ear Infections: Labyrinthitis, an infection of the inner ear, can cause dizziness due to its role in balance regulation.

More Serious Causes of Dizziness

  • Stroke or Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA): According to the CDC, dizziness can sometimes be a sign of a stroke or TIA, especially when accompanied by other symptoms like slurred speech or numbness.
  • Meniere’s Disease: According to MedlinePlus, this condition, affecting the inner ear, can cause recurrent dizziness and vertigo along with hearing loss. (More information on Meniere’s disease can be found on).
  • Vestibular Neuritis: According to NIH, inflammation of the vestibular nerve, which controls balance, can cause vertigo and dizziness.
  • Heart Problems: Arrhythmias or low blood flow to the brain can lead to dizziness or vertigo, often accompanied by chest pain or shortness of breath.

When Should Dizziness or Vertigo Be Considered an Emergency?

Key Red Flags for Emergency Care

Certain symptoms accompanying dizziness or vertigo warrant immediate medical attention. If you or a loved one experiences any of the following, don’t wait – seek emergency care immediately:

  • Severe or Sudden Vertigo: When vertigo is sudden and severe, especially if accompanied by nausea or vomiting.
  • Slurred Speech or Difficulty Understanding Speech: This could be a sign of a stroke.
  • Weakness or Numbness on One Side of the Body: This may indicate a stroke or TIA.
  • Sudden Loss of Vision: Losing vision in one or both eyes, especially with dizziness, is a red flag for serious conditions like stroke.
  • Severe Headache: A headache that doesn’t go away or is different from previous ones can signal a neurological emergency.
  • Difficulty Walking or Maintaining Balance: If the dizziness causes you to fall or have trouble staying steady, it’s important to seek medical help.

The Connection Between Stroke and Dizziness

Dizziness is a key symptom of a stroke, and recognizing this early can be life-saving. If dizziness is accompanied by other symptoms, such as weakness, slurred speech, or confusion, it’s important to treat it as a stroke until proven otherwise. Time is critical in stroke treatment; the quicker the intervention, the better the chances of recovery.

Diagnostic Tests and Treatment for Dizziness and Vertigo

How Healthcare Providers Diagnose the Cause of Dizziness

A healthcare provider will usually start by performing a physical and neurological exam to assess balance, coordination, and reflexes. Common diagnostic tools for dizziness include:

  • Balance Tests: These assess how well your inner ear, brain, and eyes work together.
  • Imaging: MRI or CT scans may be used to rule out serious conditions like strokes or tumors.
  • Blood Pressure Monitoring: Checking for sudden drops in blood pressure when standing up.
  • Heart Monitoring: If heart-related issues are suspected, an ECG or Holter monitor may be used.

Common Treatments for Dizziness and Vertigo

Treatment for dizziness or vertigo depends on the underlying cause:

  • Medications: Anti-nausea and anti-dizziness medications can help alleviate symptoms.
  • Vestibular Rehabilitation: Physical therapy exercises designed to help you regain balance and coordination.
  • Surgical Options: In cases like Meniere’s disease, surgery may be necessary to manage symptoms.

How to Manage and Prevent Dizziness and Vertigo at Home

Lifestyle Adjustments for Dizziness Prevention

  • Stay Hydrated: Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day to prevent dehydration.
  • Manage Stress: Engage in relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or meditation.
  • Eat Regularly: Skipping meals can lead to low blood sugar, which can cause dizziness.
  • Limit Alcohol and Caffeine: Both can disrupt the inner ear and lead to dizziness or vertigo.
  • Balance Exercises: Regular physical activity can help improve your balance and prevent vertigo.

Home Remedies for Mild Dizziness

For mild cases of dizziness, try:

  • Resting in a Quiet Room: Lying down in a calm space can help relieve dizziness.
  • Performing Balance Exercises: If you have benign positional vertigo, exercises like the Epley maneuver can help reposition the crystals in your inner ear and relieve symptoms.

When to Seek Professional Help

When to Call Your Doctor

If dizziness or vertigo lasts longer than a few minutes or if it worsens over time, contact your doctor. If you experience dizziness along with other symptoms like chest pain, severe headache, or weakness, seek immediate medical care.

Urgent Care vs. Emergency Care

While mild dizziness or vertigo can often be treated in a doctor’s office, if you experience more severe symptoms, it’s crucial to go to the emergency room. Quick diagnosis and treatment are vital, especially when the cause of dizziness could be life-threatening, like a stroke.

Act Fast: When Dizziness or Vertigo Becomes an Emergency

If you or a loved one is experiencing dizziness, vertigo, or any of the symptoms outlined in this blog, don’t wait; your health is too important. Contact us today to schedule a consultation with one of our specialists and get the care you need.

Whether it’s a sudden onset of dizziness, vertigo, or other symptoms, we’re here 24/7 to ensure you’re treated like family, not just a number.

What are the first signs of vertigo that could signal an emergency?

Suddenly, severe spinning sensations along with nausea, vomiting, and difficulty walking could signal an emergency.

How do I know if my dizziness is from low blood pressure or something more serious?

If dizziness occurs with fainting, nausea, or blurred vision, or lasts for an extended period, it may be time to seek professional help.

Yes, vertigo combined with weakness, slurred speech, or numbness can indicate a stroke.

What should I do if I feel lightheaded while driving?

Pull over safely and rest. If the lightheadedness persists, seek medical attention.

Are there exercises I can do at home to stop dizziness from returning?

Yes, balance exercises like the Epley maneuver can help alleviate symptoms of benign positional vertigo.

Stay hydrated, eat regularly, exercise to improve balance, and manage stress.

title.raw: What to Do for Vomiting and Diarrhea That Won't Stop
title.rendered: What to Do for Vomiting and Diarrhea That Won’t Stop

content.raw:
Vomiting and diarrhea can be incredibly distressing, especially when they persist for hours or days. Whether you’re struggling with the stomach flu, food poisoning, or another underlying condition, these symptoms can leave you feeling helpless and uncomfortable. Beyond the immediate discomfort, persistent vomiting and diarrhea can also lead to dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and other health complications, making it essential to understand how to manage them effectively. In this blog, we’ll explore the common causes of vomiting and diarrhea that won’t stop, practical steps to ease your symptoms, and when it’s time to seek medical help. With the right knowledge, you can regain control over your health and avoid the worst outcomes associated with prolonged symptoms.

Understanding Vomiting and Diarrhea

The Causes of Persistent Vomiting and Diarrhea

There are a variety of factors that could contribute to persistent vomiting and diarrhea, including:
  • Viral gastroenteritis: According to the CDC, often referred to as the "stomach flu," this is one of the most common causes of vomiting and diarrhea. It’s typically caused by viruses like norovirus and rotavirus.
  • Bacterial infections: Food poisoning is a common culprit, caused by eating contaminated food or drinking contaminated water. Common bacteria responsible include Salmonella, E. coli, and Campylobacter.
  • Other causes: Chronic conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), Crohn’s disease, or celiac disease can sometimes manifest with persistent symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea.

When Vomiting and Diarrhea Become a Concern

When these symptoms last longer than 24 to 48 hours, they can lead to serious complications, including dehydration. Prolonged vomiting and diarrhea may also signal an underlying condition that requires medical intervention. Understanding when these symptoms move from a nuisance to a medical emergency is crucial for ensuring your health and safety.

What to Do When Vomiting and Diarrhea Won’t Stop

Staying Hydrated: The Most Important Step

One of the most important aspects of recovery when dealing with persistent vomiting and diarrhea is hydration. Diarrhea and vomiting can quickly deplete the body’s water and electrolytes, making rehydration essential.
  • Oral rehydration solutions (ORS): These are specifically designed to replace both water and electrolytes. Products like Pedialyte are excellent options. Water alone won't replace these lost nutrients effectively.
  • What to avoid: Avoid sugary drinks like soda or fruit juice, which can make diarrhea worse. Similarly, caffeinated beverages and alcohol should be avoided as they can exacerbate dehydration.
  • Signs of dehydration: Keep an eye out for signs like dry mouth, dizziness, dark urine, and reduced urination. If you notice these, it’s critical to focus on hydration immediately.

Foods to Avoid and What to Eat

During a bout of vomiting and diarrhea, your stomach may be sensitive to certain foods.
  • BRAT diet: A commonly recommended eating plan that includes bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast. These foods are gentle on the stomach and easy to digest.
  • Foods to avoid: Fatty, spicy, or dairy-heavy foods should be avoided as they can worsen symptoms.
  • Gradual reintroduction: Once vomiting has stopped, gradually begin eating solid foods again. Start with bland options and slowly reintroduce more varied foods as tolerated.

Resting and Managing Your Symptoms at Home

In addition to managing hydration and nutrition, resting is essential for your body’s recovery.
  • Physical rest: Allowing your body to recover is critical, so avoid strenuous activities until symptoms subside.
  • Over-the-counter medications: According to NIDDK, anti-nausea or anti-diarrheal medications (such as Imodium or Pepto-Bismol) may help alleviate symptoms. However, they should be used cautiously and avoided if you have a fever or blood in your stool.
  • Managing fever: If you have a fever, use acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen to help reduce it, but always follow dosing instructions.

When Should You Seek Medical Attention?

Warning Signs That Require Immediate Medical Help

If you experience any of the following, it’s essential to seek medical attention as soon as possible:
  • Severe dehydration: Symptoms include dry mouth, sunken eyes, dizziness, and very dark urine.
  • Blood in vomit or stool: If you notice blood in your vomit or stool, it could indicate a more serious condition, such as an ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • High fever or prolonged symptoms: A fever above 101°F (38.3°C) or symptoms lasting more than 48 hours warrant a visit to the doctor.

Special Considerations for Vulnerable Groups

Certain groups are at a higher risk of complications from vomiting and diarrhea, including:
  • Infants and young children: They can become dehydrated more quickly and may need medical treatment sooner.
  • Elderly individuals: Older adults are more vulnerable to dehydration, and prolonged symptoms can exacerbate underlying conditions.
  • People with pre-existing health conditions: If you have conditions like diabetes or heart disease, persistent vomiting and diarrhea may complicate your health, making it crucial to seek medical advice sooner.

Prevention: How to Avoid Future Episodes of Vomiting and Diarrhea

Hygiene and Safe Food Handling

Preventing future episodes of vomiting and diarrhea comes down to hygiene and proper food safety.
  • Wash your hands: Always wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water, especially after using the bathroom or handling food.
  • Food safety: Practice safe food handling, including cooking meat to the proper temperature, washing fruits and vegetables, and avoiding consumption of raw or undercooked foods.

Vaccines and Probiotics

  • Norovirus prevention: While there’s no vaccine for all types of vomiting and diarrhea, practicing proper hygiene can significantly reduce your risk of norovirus infection.
  • Probiotics: Taking probiotics may help support your gut health and reduce the severity and frequency of gastrointestinal issues.

Need Relief from Vomiting and Diarrhea? Book a Consultation Today!

If you're experiencing persistent vomiting and diarrhea, don't wait! Our team at ER of Lufkin is ready to provide expert care and help you recover quickly. Whether you're dealing with dehydration, severe symptoms, or other concerns, we’re here for you. Visit the ER of Lufkin now for fast relief and expert care. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What causes vomiting and diarrhea to last for more than 24 hours?

Common causes include viral infections like norovirus or bacterial infections from contaminated food or water.

Can dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea cause serious complications?

Yes, dehydration can lead to kidney failure and other life-threatening issues, especially in vulnerable groups like children and the elderly.

What are the signs that my diarrhea or vomiting is caused by a viral infection?

Typical signs include sudden onset, vomiting followed by diarrhea, and possible fever. The infection usually resolves on its own within a few days.

How can I treat diarrhea and vomiting at home?

Focus on staying hydrated with oral rehydration solutions, rest, and gradually reintroducing bland foods like the BRAT diet.

Is it safe to take anti-diarrheal medications?

Anti-diarrheal medications may help control symptoms but should be used with caution. Avoid them if you have a high fever or blood in your stool.

When should I seek medical attention for vomiting and diarrhea?

If symptoms persist beyond 48 hours, if you're unable to stay hydrated, or if you notice severe symptoms like blood in vomit or stool, seek medical care.

What can I do to prevent vomiting and diarrhea in the future?

Practice good hygiene, avoid contaminated food and water, and ensure proper food handling to prevent gastrointestinal infections.
