title.raw: ER vs. Urgent Care: How to Make the Right Choice for Your Health in Lufkin
title.rendered: ER vs. Urgent Care: How to Make the Right Choice for Your Health in Lufkin

content.raw:
Medically Reviewed by: the ER of Lufkin clinical team | Updated: July 2026

It’s 8 PM on a Tuesday, and your child has a high fever and a cough that just won’t quit. Or maybe you’ve just sliced your hand while cooking dinner, and it looks deep. In that moment of pain or panic, a dozen questions flood your mind. "Is this serious? Do I need the emergency room? What if I go and it's not an emergency? What if I don't go... and it is?" You’re not alone. In our Lufkin community, we see families facing this stressful decision every single day. Making the right choice is confusing, especially when you're worried about a loved one's health, the long wait times, or the high cost of an emergency room visit.

How Do I Tell If I Should Go to the ER or Urgent Care? The Core Difference

Let’s start with the simplest, most important distinction. Think of it this way: An Emergency Room (ER) is for conditions that threaten your life, a limb, or your eyesight. An Urgent Care center is for illnesses or injuries that need prompt medical attention (within 24 hours) but are not life-threatening. Our "rule of thumb" is this: If you’d normally see your primary care doctor for your condition, but you can't get a same-day appointment or it's after hours, urgent care is your best bet. It’s the perfect "in-between" option. If your condition is severe, came on suddenly, and makes you think "this could be permanent or fatal," that is an emergency. Your decision really comes down to three key factors:
  1. Severity of Symptoms: Is this a threat to your life or long-term health? (e.g., chest pain vs. a sprained ankle).
  2. Services Needed: Does the condition require advanced, hospital-level resources like a CT scan, blood transfusion, or immediate surgery?
  3. Cost & Time: Emergency rooms are legally required to be open 24/7/365 and staffed to handle life-or-death situations. That level of readiness is expensive, and visits are priced accordingly. They also don't work on a first-come, first-served basis; they work on triage, meaning the most severe patients are seen first. Urgent care centers are designed for convenience, speed, and affordability for those "in-between" issues.

When Should You Go to the ER? Signs of a True Emergency

This is the most critical part of the equation. When it comes to a potential emergency, the most important advice we can give is this: Trust your gut. If it feels life-threatening, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room in Lufkin immediately. It is always better to be safe than sorry. According to MedlinePlus, a U.S. National Library of Medicine service, an emergency is any condition where a delay in seeking medical attention could be hazardous to your life or health. If you are experiencing any of these symptoms, do not drive yourself. Call 911.

Go to the ER for Symptoms That Threaten Life or Limb

  • Chest Pain or Difficulty Breathing: This is at the top of the list for a reason. Any severe chest pain, pressure, or squeezing, especially if it's accompanied by shortness of breath, nausea, or pain radiating to your arm, jaw, or back, could be a heart attack.
  • Signs of a Stroke: Remember the F.A.S.T. acronym:
F - Face Drooping: Is one side of the face numb or drooping? A - Arm Weakness: Is one arm weak, numb, or drifting downward? S - Speech Difficulty: Is speech slurred or difficult to understand? T - Time to Call 911: Every second counts.
  • Severe, Uncontrolled Bleeding: Any bleeding that does not slow or stop after 10-15 minutes of firm, direct pressure.
  • Sudden, Severe Pain: This includes a "thunderclap" headache that comes on instantly and is the worst pain of your life, or sudden, severe abdominal pain.
  • Loss of Consciousness or Seizures: Any fainting, passing out (even if you wake up quickly), or a seizure, especially if it's a first-time seizure.
  • Major Injuries or Trauma:
    • Any significant head, neck, or spine injury, especially from a car accident or a fall.
    • Major broken bones, like a bone that is visibly out of place or an open fracture.
    • A deep wound or bad cut.
    • Severe burns, especially large burns or any burns on the hands, feet, face, or groin.
  • High Fever with Other Symptoms: A high, persistent fever accompanied by a stiff neck, mental confusion, or a severe rash.
  • Mental Health Crisis: If you or a loved one is having suicidal thoughts or is actively a danger to themselves or others. (You can also call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline 24/7).

When to Use Urgent Care: The "In-Between" Medical Needs

Now, let's talk about the wide range of issues that are perfect for an urgent care center. These conditions are painful, disruptive, and need to be seen, but they aren't emergencies. Urgent care is the bridge between your primary care physician (PCP) and the ER. When your Lufkin PCP is booked for the day, or it's a Saturday afternoon and you roll your ankle, urgent care is there for you.

Go to Urgent Care for Common Illnesses and Minor Injuries

  • Fevers, Colds, and Flu: You feel miserable, your fever is 101°F, and you have body aches. Urgent care can test you for the flu or strep and provide treatment to help you recover.
  • Minor Cuts and Burns: That kitchen knife slip that probably needs a few stitches but isn't gushing blood. Or a painful, blistering (but small) burn from a hot pan.
  • Sprains and Strains: You rolled your ankle playing basketball, and it's swollen and painful. You need an X-ray to make sure it's not a break, but your life isn't in danger.
  • Minor Broken Bones: A suspected broken finger or toe. Urgent care centers are equipped with X-ray machines to diagnose these common injuries.
  • Infections: This is a big one. Urgent care is ideal for:
    • Painful ear infections
    • Sore throats (they can do a rapid strep test)
    • Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)
    • Pink eye
    • Skin infections, rashes, or insect bites
  • Vomiting or Diarrhea: If you have a stomach bug and are worried about getting dehydrated, urgent care can help.

The Benefits of Choosing Urgent Care in Lufkin

When you choose urgent care for these conditions, you're not just making a good choice for yourself; you're helping our whole community.
  • You Save Time: The biggest difference you'll feel is the wait. In an ER, a sprained ankle will always wait behind chest pain. That's triage. At urgent care, your sprained ankle is the priority, and you'll be seen much more quickly.
  • You Save Money: As Medicare outlines, the cost for "urgently needed care" is typically far lower than for "emergency department services." An ER visit often includes a high "facility fee" on top of the doctor's bill. An urgent care co-pay is usually a fraction of that cost.
  • You Get the Right Level of Care: By choosing wisely, you free up our local Lufkin emergency rooms and their specialized teams to focus on the truly life-threatening cases.

What Can the ER Do That Urgent Care Can't? Understanding the Limitations

It's helpful to think of the ER and urgent care as two different tools. An urgent care center is like a high-quality, well-stocked toolbox. An emergency room is a full-service auto garage with specialized, heavy-duty equipment. It's not about one being "better," it's about having the right tool for the job.

"The emergency room is by definition capable of dealing with all manner of emergencies, be they mild and merely painful to life-threatening, whereas an urgent care is much more structured to deal with what we call lower-acuity or more minor complaints which nonetheless need to be addressed, such as sore throats, lacerations, maybe sprains, simple fractures, things like that."

Dr. Robert Stephen, emergency room physician at the University of Utah, in a University of Utah Health interview

Services are ONLY Available at an Emergency Room

Urgent care centers have limitations. They are not equipped to handle life-or-death situations. The ER is, because it's almost always part of a larger hospital.
  • Advanced Imaging: While most Lufkin urgent care centers have X-rays, ERs have 24/7 access to CT scanners (for diagnosing strokes, head injuries, or internal bleeding) and MRIs.
  • Life-Saving Interventions: This is the big one. ERs are staffed and equipped for resuscitation, intubation (placing a breathing tube), blood transfusions, and have immediate access to an operating room.
  • Admission to the Hospital: An urgent care center is a standalone clinic. If your condition is serious, they cannot admit you to the hospital. The ER is the "front door" to the hospital; the admission process starts there.
  • Specialist Access: In an ER, the doctor can get a cardiologist, a neurosurgeon, or a general surgeon to your bedside in minutes for a critical consultation.

What Happens If I Go to Urgent Care with an Emergency?

This is a common fear, and we want to put your mind at ease. You are not a doctor, and it's not your job to be 100% right every time. If you go to an urgent care center with symptoms of a heart attack, the medical team is trained to recognize that emergency immediately. They will not try to treat you. They will stabilize you, call 911, and get you transported to the nearest emergency room. You will not be in trouble for "choosing wrong." The most important thing is that you sought help.

A Quick-Reference Chart: ER vs. Urgent Care

For our mobile readers and visual learners, here’s a simple chart to help you make a quick decision.
Condition Go to Urgent Care Go to the Emergency Room (ER)
Breathing Mild cough, cold, or wheezing Severe difficulty breathing, shortness of breath
Pain Sore throat, earache, mild headache Severe chest pain, severe abdominal pain, "worst headache of your life"
Injury Sprain, minor cut, minor burn, twisted ankle Major broken bone (visible deformity), head/spine injury, severe burn
Bleeding Minor cut that needs stitches Bleeding that won't stop after 10-15 min. of pressure
Other Fever/flu, UTI, rash, vomiting Loss of consciousness, stroke symptoms (F.A.S.T.), seizures

Get the Right Care, Right When You Need It

We hope this guide makes your next step clearer. When it is an emergency, or you're not sure whether it is one, ER of Lufkin is ready 24/7. Just walk in, no appointment needed. Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What’s the difference between ER and Urgent Care?

ER handles life-threatening emergencies; Urgent Care treats minor illnesses and injuries that need quick attention but aren’t severe.

When should I go to Urgent Care?

Go for things like fever, flu, ear infections, sprains, minor cuts, or mild fractures.

When should I go to the ER?

Head to the ER for chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke signs, heavy bleeding, or major injuries.

Which one costs more?

ER visits usually cost more and take longer, while Urgent Care is faster and more affordable.

Can Urgent Care do X-rays or labs?

Yes, most centers offer basic X-rays, labs, and stitches, but serious conditions need the ER.

What if I’m unsure?

If symptoms feel severe or sudden, go to the ER or call 911 to stay safe.

Does insurance cover both?

Most plans cover both, but co-pays and costs are lower at Urgent Care for non-emergencies.

Can kids go to Urgent Care?

Yes, most treat both adults and children for minor illnesses and injuries.
content.rendered:
Medically Reviewed by: the ER of Lufkin clinical team | Updated: July 2026

It’s 8 PM on a Tuesday, and your child has a high fever and a cough that just won’t quit. Or maybe you’ve just sliced your hand while cooking dinner, and it looks deep.

In that moment of pain or panic, a dozen questions flood your mind. “Is this serious? Do I need the emergency room? What if I go and it’s not an emergency? What if I don’t go… and it is?”

You’re not alone. In our Lufkin community, we see families facing this stressful decision every single day. Making the right choice is confusing, especially when you’re worried about a loved one’s health, the long wait times, or the high cost of an emergency room visit.

How Do I Tell If I Should Go to the ER or Urgent Care? The Core Difference

Let’s start with the simplest, most important distinction.

Think of it this way: An Emergency Room (ER) is for conditions that threaten your life, a limb, or your eyesight.

An Urgent Care center is for illnesses or injuries that need prompt medical attention (within 24 hours) but are not life-threatening.

Our “rule of thumb” is this: If you’d normally see your primary care doctor for your condition, but you can’t get a same-day appointment or it’s after hours, urgent care is your best bet. It’s the perfect “in-between” option.

If your condition is severe, came on suddenly, and makes you think “this could be permanent or fatal,” that is an emergency.

Your decision really comes down to three key factors:

  1. Severity of Symptoms: Is this a threat to your life or long-term health? (e.g., chest pain vs. a sprained ankle).
  2. Services Needed: Does the condition require advanced, hospital-level resources like a CT scan, blood transfusion, or immediate surgery?
  3. Cost & Time: Emergency rooms are legally required to be open 24/7/365 and staffed to handle life-or-death situations. That level of readiness is expensive, and visits are priced accordingly. They also don’t work on a first-come, first-served basis; they work on triage, meaning the most severe patients are seen first. Urgent care centers are designed for convenience, speed, and affordability for those “in-between” issues.

When Should You Go to the ER? Signs of a True Emergency

This is the most critical part of the equation. When it comes to a potential emergency, the most important advice we can give is this: Trust your gut. If it feels life-threatening, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room in Lufkin immediately.

It is always better to be safe than sorry.

According to MedlinePlus, a U.S. National Library of Medicine service, an emergency is any condition where a delay in seeking medical attention could be hazardous to your life or health.

If you are experiencing any of these symptoms, do not drive yourself. Call 911.

Go to the ER for Symptoms That Threaten Life or Limb

  • Chest Pain or Difficulty Breathing: This is at the top of the list for a reason. Any severe chest pain, pressure, or squeezing, especially if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, nausea, or pain radiating to your arm, jaw, or back, could be a heart attack.
  • Signs of a Stroke: Remember the F.A.S.T. acronym:

F – Face Drooping: Is one side of the face numb or drooping?

A – Arm Weakness: Is one arm weak, numb, or drifting downward?

S – Speech Difficulty: Is speech slurred or difficult to understand?

T – Time to Call 911: Every second counts.

  • Severe, Uncontrolled Bleeding: Any bleeding that does not slow or stop after 10-15 minutes of firm, direct pressure.
  • Sudden, Severe Pain: This includes a “thunderclap” headache that comes on instantly and is the worst pain of your life, or sudden, severe abdominal pain.
  • Loss of Consciousness or Seizures: Any fainting, passing out (even if you wake up quickly), or a seizure, especially if it’s a first-time seizure.
  • Major Injuries or Trauma:
    • Any significant head, neck, or spine injury, especially from a car accident or a fall.
    • Major broken bones, like a bone that is visibly out of place or an open fracture.
    • A deep wound or bad cut.
    • Severe burns, especially large burns or any burns on the hands, feet, face, or groin.
  • High Fever with Other Symptoms: A high, persistent fever accompanied by a stiff neck, mental confusion, or a severe rash.
  • Mental Health Crisis: If you or a loved one is having suicidal thoughts or is actively a danger to themselves or others. (You can also call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline 24/7).

When to Use Urgent Care: The “In-Between” Medical Needs

Now, let’s talk about the wide range of issues that are perfect for an urgent care center. These conditions are painful, disruptive, and need to be seen, but they aren’t emergencies. Urgent care is the bridge between your primary care physician (PCP) and the ER.

When your Lufkin PCP is booked for the day, or it’s a Saturday afternoon and you roll your ankle, urgent care is there for you.

Go to Urgent Care for Common Illnesses and Minor Injuries

  • Fevers, Colds, and Flu: You feel miserable, your fever is 101°F, and you have body aches. Urgent care can test you for the flu or strep and provide treatment to help you recover.
  • Minor Cuts and Burns: That kitchen knife slip that probably needs a few stitches but isn’t gushing blood. Or a painful, blistering (but small) burn from a hot pan.
  • Sprains and Strains: You rolled your ankle playing basketball, and it’s swollen and painful. You need an X-ray to make sure it’s not a break, but your life isn’t in danger.
  • Minor Broken Bones: A suspected broken finger or toe. Urgent care centers are equipped with X-ray machines to diagnose these common injuries.
  • Infections: This is a big one. Urgent care is ideal for:
    • Painful ear infections
    • Sore throats (they can do a rapid strep test)
    • Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)
    • Pink eye
    • Skin infections, rashes, or insect bites
  • Vomiting or Diarrhea: If you have a stomach bug and are worried about getting dehydrated, urgent care can help.

The Benefits of Choosing Urgent Care in Lufkin

When you choose urgent care for these conditions, you’re not just making a good choice for yourself; you’re helping our whole community.

  • You Save Time: The biggest difference you’ll feel is the wait. In an ER, a sprained ankle will always wait behind chest pain. That’s triage. At urgent care, your sprained ankle is the priority, and you’ll be seen much more quickly.
  • You Save Money: As Medicare outlines, the cost for “urgently needed care” is typically far lower than for “emergency department services.” An ER visit often includes a high “facility fee” on top of the doctor’s bill. An urgent care co-pay is usually a fraction of that cost.
  • You Get the Right Level of Care: By choosing wisely, you free up our local Lufkin emergency rooms and their specialized teams to focus on the truly life-threatening cases.

What Can the ER Do That Urgent Care Can’t? Understanding the Limitations

It’s helpful to think of the ER and urgent care as two different tools. An urgent care center is like a high-quality, well-stocked toolbox. An emergency room is a full-service auto garage with specialized, heavy-duty equipment.

It’s not about one being “better,” it’s about having the right tool for the job.

“The emergency room is by definition capable of dealing with all manner of emergencies, be they mild and merely painful to life-threatening, whereas an urgent care is much more structured to deal with what we call lower-acuity or more minor complaints which nonetheless need to be addressed, such as sore throats, lacerations, maybe sprains, simple fractures, things like that.”

Dr. Robert Stephen, emergency room physician at the University of Utah, in a University of Utah Health interview

Services are ONLY Available at an Emergency Room

Urgent care centers have limitations. They are not equipped to handle life-or-death situations. The ER is, because it’s almost always part of a larger hospital.

  • Advanced Imaging: While most Lufkin urgent care centers have X-rays, ERs have 24/7 access to CT scanners (for diagnosing strokes, head injuries, or internal bleeding) and MRIs.
  • Life-Saving Interventions: This is the big one. ERs are staffed and equipped for resuscitation, intubation (placing a breathing tube), blood transfusions, and have immediate access to an operating room.
  • Admission to the Hospital: An urgent care center is a standalone clinic. If your condition is serious, they cannot admit you to the hospital. The ER is the “front door” to the hospital; the admission process starts there.
  • Specialist Access: In an ER, the doctor can get a cardiologist, a neurosurgeon, or a general surgeon to your bedside in minutes for a critical consultation.

What Happens If I Go to Urgent Care with an Emergency?

This is a common fear, and we want to put your mind at ease. You are not a doctor, and it’s not your job to be 100% right every time.

If you go to an urgent care center with symptoms of a heart attack, the medical team is trained to recognize that emergency immediately. They will not try to treat you. They will stabilize you, call 911, and get you transported to the nearest emergency room. You will not be in trouble for “choosing wrong.” The most important thing is that you sought help.

A Quick-Reference Chart: ER vs. Urgent Care

For our mobile readers and visual learners, here’s a simple chart to help you make a quick decision.

Condition Go to Urgent Care Go to the Emergency Room (ER)
Breathing Mild cough, cold, or wheezing Severe difficulty breathing, shortness of breath
Pain Sore throat, earache, mild headache Severe chest pain, severe abdominal pain, “worst headache of your life”
Injury Sprain, minor cut, minor burn, twisted ankle Major broken bone (visible deformity), head/spine injury, severe burn
Bleeding Minor cut that needs stitches Bleeding that won’t stop after 10-15 min. of pressure
Other Fever/flu, UTI, rash, vomiting Loss of consciousness, stroke symptoms (F.A.S.T.), seizures

Get the Right Care, Right When You Need It

We hope this guide makes your next step clearer. When it is an emergency, or you’re not sure whether it is one, ER of Lufkin is ready 24/7. Just walk in, no appointment needed.

Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands.

Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313

Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What’s the difference between ER and Urgent Care?

ER handles life-threatening emergencies; Urgent Care treats minor illnesses and injuries that need quick attention but aren’t severe.

When should I go to Urgent Care?

Go for things like fever, flu, ear infections, sprains, minor cuts, or mild fractures.

When should I go to the ER?

Head to the ER for chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke signs, heavy bleeding, or major injuries.

Which one costs more?

ER visits usually cost more and take longer, while Urgent Care is faster and more affordable.

Can Urgent Care do X-rays or labs?

Yes, most centers offer basic X-rays, labs, and stitches, but serious conditions need the ER.

What if I’m unsure?

If symptoms feel severe or sudden, go to the ER or call 911 to stay safe.

Does insurance cover both?

Most plans cover both, but co-pays and costs are lower at Urgent Care for non-emergencies.

Can kids go to Urgent Care?

Yes, most treat both adults and children for minor illnesses and injuries.

title.raw: Pediatric Care: Essential for Your Child's Health and Development
title.rendered: Pediatric Care: Essential for Your Child’s Health and Development

content.raw:
Parenting and caregiving are the most significant responsibilities, as parents and caregivers ensure the health and safety of our kids.  Pediatric care is not only about the treatment of sickness, but also assists a child in his/her physical, emotional, and mental maturation. To infants and adolescents, children require attention.  Routine checkups, vaccinations, and assistance in unforeseen issues are guaranteed to ensure that kids become healthy adults.  This blog will give you reasons as to why pediatric care is important, how it will benefit your child, and what you can do to ensure your child receives the appropriate care.

What Is Pediatric Care?

Pediatric care is healthcare that concerns itself with the special needs of children between birth and their teenage years. Pediatricians are aware of how to diagnose and treat specific problems as opposed to general doctors. Pediatric care covers:
  • Preventive care: checkups, immunizations, and growth screening.
  • Management of chronic conditions, asthma, diabetes, and allergies.
  • Acute care: Treatment for common childhood illnesses like colds, infections, and injuries.
  • Specialized care: Addressing behavioral, developmental, and emotional health needs.
Pediatricians are not just doctors; they are consultants to the parents, and they demonstrate how to handle the health of the child in a transparent manner.

Key Components of Pediatric Care

Regular Check-ups & Growth Monitoring

Pediatricians monitor the growth and development of the kids at each stage. Such visits can lead to the identification of issues at their initial stages, such as development delays, hearing or vision issues, or an unhealthy diet.

Vaccinations and Immunizations

According to the CDC, one of the primary responsibilities of pediatric care involves ensuring that children receive the necessary vaccines to protect them against such serious illnesses as polio, measles, and whooping cough.

Sick Visits and Acute Care

Children are prone to colds, influenza, and ear infections. Pediatricians cure such diseases and prevent potential risk factors.

Chronic Condition Management

Pediatric care implies long-term care and support to those children with such chronic diseases as asthma, diabetes, or ADHD. Practitioners collaborate with the parents and other experts in developing a care plan that will suit the needs of the child.

Behavioral and Mental Health Support

The NIH claims that due to the increased mental health awareness, pediatric care now also approaches the feelings and behavior issues, including anxiety, depression, or even such disorders as ADHD.

The Role of a Pediatrician in Your Child's Health Journey

The pediatrician is not only a health service provider, but he or she is also a companion in the health of the child. They advise on healthy lifestyle, nutrition, safety, and even parenthood. With the help of establishing a strong bond with a child and parents, they form trust and stability. Frequent visits allow parents to be informed enough and make healthy decisions concerning their child.

Common Pediatric Health Concerns

Every stage of childhood brings different health challenges. Some of the most common concerns parents face include:
  • Fevers: A common symptom of many childhood illnesses.
  • Ear infections: Especially common in young children, they can cause pain and discomfort.
  • Respiratory issues: Asthma, bronchitis, and colds are frequent in children.
  • Skin rashes: From diaper rashes to more serious conditions like eczema.
  • Behavioral issues: Difficulty focusing or managing emotions can impact a child’s school life and social development.
Understanding these concerns can help parents seek timely care and avoid unnecessary anxiety.

How to Choose the Right Pediatrician for Your Child

Choosing a pediatrician is a tremendous choice. Identify a doctor who will address the health care needs of your child, and also suit your family values and parenting model. Consider the following:
  • Credentials and experience:  Find a board-certified pediatrician who has experience.
  • Accessibility: Select a pediatrician with flexible working hours and accessible in cases of emergency.
  • Communication style: The doctor must listen to you and clarify things.
  • Location and convenience: Proximity to your home or workplace can make regular visits easier.
It is only with careful consideration of these factors that you will be able to provide your child with the best care possible.

Pediatric Care at Different Stages of Development

Newborn & Infant Care

During the first year, the pediatrics is concerned with monitoring development, administering immunizations, and assisting parents with nutrition and sleep. Pediatricians also observe such milestones as crawling and walking.

Toddler & Early Childhood Care

Between the ages of 1 and 5, children run around and pose numerous questions, and this may lead to injuries. Pediatricians continue with vaccines, observing growth and speech, motor skill,s and behavioral assistance.

School-Age and Adolescent Care

Pediatric care includes frequent checkups, treatment of chronic illnesses, and mental health since the age of 6 to 18. Children also get to know more, and may require emotional support.

Why Preventive Care is Key in Pediatric Health

According to the CDC, preventive care is highly significant to children. Serious problems can be prevented with the help of vaccines, frequent checkups, and the early observation of health problems. You provide the best opportunity to live a healthy life to your child by developing healthy habits and seeking early care.

Give Your Child the Care They Deserve

From accidents to unexpected illnesses, our pediatric ER is always ready to provide fast, expert treatment for your little one. Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

At what age should I take my child for their first pediatric checkup?

It’s recommended that your baby see a pediatrician within the first week of life to monitor growth and development.

What vaccinations does my child need?

Your child will need several vaccines starting from infancy to protect against diseases like measles, polio, and influenza.

How can I tell if my child’s behavior is normal or a sign of a problem?

Behavioral changes can be normal as children grow, but a pediatrician can help identify if there’s an underlying issue.

How often should I schedule checkups for my child?

Children typically need a checkup every year. More frequent visits are necessary for babies, especially in the first year.

What should I do if my child is sick after office hours?

Many pediatricians offer after-hours care or have on-call services for emergencies.

Does pediatric care cover mental health services?

Yes, pediatric care includes mental health support for issues such as anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

How can I prepare my child for a pediatric appointment?

Be sure to explain to your child what to expect and make the visit feel like a positive experience.

Does ER of Lufkin treat Pediatric Care?

Yes, ER of Lufkin treats Pediatric Care. We provide the highest level of medical care in a child-friendly environment, ensuring both young patients and their families feel comfortable during stressful situations.

title.raw: Poisoning and Overdose: Symptoms, Treatment, and When to Seek Emergency Care
title.rendered: Poisoning and Overdose: Symptoms, Treatment, and When to Seek Emergency Care

content.raw:
The use of poisoning and overdose cases is increasingly becoming common in the U.S., and that is a major danger to the health of the people.  It has been reported that one of the leading causes of death in the country is now a drug overdose, and an overdose with opioids is a significant portion of it.  In addition to damaging the body, poisoning and overdoses cause severe emotional and mental issues to family members and loved ones. The information about the definition of poisoning and overdose, the reasons why they occur, the ability to identify whether they occur or not, and the actions to be undertaken to prevent such tragic events is crucial.  This blog will present you with the most important information that can help you do the right thing in case of poisoning or overdose.

What is Poisoning and Overdose?

Defining Poisoning and Overdose

According to the CDC, poisoning occurs when a harmful substance, such as a chemical, a drug, or a toxin, enters the body in excessive amounts and damages it. According to Medline, overdose specifically refers to taking more than the recommended or safe amount of a substance, leading to dangerous or fatal outcomes. Although the two terms are used interchangeably, in some cases, they may not have the same meaning. Poisoning occurs if a person ingests a dangerous chemical by mistake, whereas an overdose is considered to be associated with the misuse of drugs. Poisoning may be unintentional, as witnessed in children, or intentional, as witnessed in drug overdoses.

Types of Substances Involved in Poisoning and Overdose

Some of the most common substances involved in poisoning and overdose incidents include:
  • Household chemicals (e.g., cleaning supplies, pesticides)
  • Medications (over-the-counter and prescription drugs)
  • Alcohol and illicit drugs
  • Carbon monoxide and other gases
  • Narcotics and opioids, such as heroin and fentanyl, have contributed to the opioid crisis.
The problem of opioid overdoses has become extremely severe, and the primary drug implicated in the majority of the overdose-related cases is fentanyl. SAMHSA (2021) reports that nearly 80% of the total opioid-related deaths in the U.S. were fentanyl.

How Poisoning and Overdose Happen

Unintentional Poisoning

Most poisoning incidents are unintentional, particularly in children who may ingest toxic substances out of curiosity. Adults are also exposed to poisoning when storing or poorly dealing with household chemicals or abusing drugs.

Intentional Poisoning and Overdose

Individuals intending to overdose, like in suicide attempts, are also of great concern. Individuals with psychiatric conditions are likely to overdose in an attempt to kill themselves. Intentional overdoses are often done with opioid drugs, including prescription painkillers, heroin, and fentanyl.

Signs and Symptoms of Poisoning and Overdose

Common Symptoms of Poisoning

  • Mild Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, and stomach pain.
  • Severe Symptoms: Difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, altered mental state, and bluish skin or lips (due to lack of oxygen).
  • Critical Symptoms: Seizures, loss of consciousness, and death in extreme cases.

Symptoms of Drug Overdose

Overdose symptoms vary based on the type of substance consumed. Common signs include:
  • Opioid overdose: Pinpoint pupils, slow or shallow breathing, and unresponsiveness.
  • Stimulant overdose (e.g., cocaine, methamphetamine): Agitation, rapid heart rate, sweating, and seizures.
  • Benzodiazepine overdose (e.g., Xanax, Valium): Drowsiness, confusion, difficulty breathing, and coma.

How to Respond to Poisoning or Overdose

Immediate Actions to Take

  • For Poisoning: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 immediately. If possible, identify the substance, how much was ingested, and when it happened.
  • For Overdose: Call 911 right away, and if the person is unconscious but breathing, try to keep them awake and sitting up if possible. For opioid overdoses, administer naloxone (Narcan) if available.

When to Seek Medical Help

When in doubt, call 911. If a person is unconscious, struggling to breathe, or showing signs of severe poisoning or overdose, medical intervention is crucial.

Prevention of Poisoning and Overdose

Preventing Accidental Poisoning

  • Store chemicals and medications out of children’s reach.
  • Properly dispose of unused or expired medications. You can find local take-back programs via the DEA.
  • Educate children and adults on the dangers of household substances.

Preventing Overdose

  • Use medications exactly as prescribed and never share prescription drugs.
  • Properly dispose of unused narcotics and opioids.
  • Advocate for the use of naloxone (Narcan) in homes where someone may be at risk for opioid overdose.
  • Encourage access to mental health support for individuals who may be at risk of intentional overdose.

Mental Health Support and Suicide Prevention

Most of the overdoses are accidental, but others are triggered by emotional and mental health problems. Addressing the underlying factors, such as depression and suicidal ideation, is life-saving. In case of a possible risk to a person you know, contact a specialist in mental health.

Learn More About Overdose Prevention

Protect yourself and your family by understanding how to safely store medications, recognize overdose symptoms, and seek support.  Contact us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance to learn how we can help you prevent poisoning and overdose in your home. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Can poisoning or overdose be reversed?

Yes, many can be reversed with quick medical treatment, like naloxone for opioid overdoses.

How can I prevent accidental poisoning?

Store chemicals and medications safely, and dispose of unused items properly.

What is naloxone, and how does it work?

Naloxone reverses opioid overdoses by blocking the effects of opioids on the brain, especially slowing breathing.

Are all overdoses intentional?

Not all; many overdoses are accidental, especially with medications or household chemicals.

What are the signs of overdose?

Symptoms include unconsciousness, slow breathing, confusion, and seizures. Seek immediate medical help.

How can poisoning be prevented?

Properly store hazardous substances and educate others about their risks.

Does ER of Lufkin treat poisoning and overdose?

Yes, the ER of Lufkin treats poisoning and overdose. ER of Lufkin is equipped to treat both poisoning and overdose cases.

The information about the definition of poisoning and overdose, the reasons why they occur, the ability to identify whether they occur or not, and the actions to be undertaken to prevent such tragic events is crucial. 

This blog will present you with the most important information that can help you do the right thing in case of poisoning or overdose.

What is Poisoning and Overdose?

Defining Poisoning and Overdose

According to the CDC, poisoning occurs when a harmful substance, such as a chemical, a drug, or a toxin, enters the body in excessive amounts and damages it.

According to Medline, overdose specifically refers to taking more than the recommended or safe amount of a substance, leading to dangerous or fatal outcomes. Although the two terms are used interchangeably, in some cases, they may not have the same meaning.

Poisoning occurs if a person ingests a dangerous chemical by mistake, whereas an overdose is considered to be associated with the misuse of drugs.

Poisoning may be unintentional, as witnessed in children, or intentional, as witnessed in drug overdoses.

Types of Substances Involved in Poisoning and Overdose

Some of the most common substances involved in poisoning and overdose incidents include:

  • Household chemicals (e.g., cleaning supplies, pesticides)
  • Medications (over-the-counter and prescription drugs)
  • Alcohol and illicit drugs
  • Carbon monoxide and other gases
  • Narcotics and opioids, such as heroin and fentanyl, have contributed to the opioid crisis.

The problem of opioid overdoses has become extremely severe, and the primary drug implicated in the majority of the overdose-related cases is fentanyl. SAMHSA (2021) reports that nearly 80% of the total opioid-related deaths in the U.S. were fentanyl.

How Poisoning and Overdose Happen

Unintentional Poisoning

Most poisoning incidents are unintentional, particularly in children who may ingest toxic substances out of curiosity. Adults are also exposed to poisoning when storing or poorly dealing with household chemicals or abusing drugs.

Intentional Poisoning and Overdose

Individuals intending to overdose, like in suicide attempts, are also of great concern. Individuals with psychiatric conditions are likely to overdose in an attempt to kill themselves. Intentional overdoses are often done with opioid drugs, including prescription painkillers, heroin, and fentanyl.

Signs and Symptoms of Poisoning and Overdose

Common Symptoms of Poisoning

  • Mild Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, and stomach pain.
  • Severe Symptoms: Difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, altered mental state, and bluish skin or lips (due to lack of oxygen).
  • Critical Symptoms: Seizures, loss of consciousness, and death in extreme cases.

Symptoms of Drug Overdose

Overdose symptoms vary based on the type of substance consumed. Common signs include:

  • Opioid overdose: Pinpoint pupils, slow or shallow breathing, and unresponsiveness.
  • Stimulant overdose (e.g., cocaine, methamphetamine): Agitation, rapid heart rate, sweating, and seizures.
  • Benzodiazepine overdose (e.g., Xanax, Valium): Drowsiness, confusion, difficulty breathing, and coma.

How to Respond to Poisoning or Overdose

Immediate Actions to Take

  • For Poisoning: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 immediately. If possible, identify the substance, how much was ingested, and when it happened.
  • For Overdose: Call 911 right away, and if the person is unconscious but breathing, try to keep them awake and sitting up if possible. For opioid overdoses, administer naloxone (Narcan) if available.

When to Seek Medical Help

When in doubt, call 911. If a person is unconscious, struggling to breathe, or showing signs of severe poisoning or overdose, medical intervention is crucial.

Prevention of Poisoning and Overdose

Preventing Accidental Poisoning

  • Store chemicals and medications out of children’s reach.
  • Properly dispose of unused or expired medications. You can find local take-back programs via the DEA.
  • Educate children and adults on the dangers of household substances.

Preventing Overdose

  • Use medications exactly as prescribed and never share prescription drugs.
  • Properly dispose of unused narcotics and opioids.
  • Advocate for the use of naloxone (Narcan) in homes where someone may be at risk for opioid overdose.
  • Encourage access to mental health support for individuals who may be at risk of intentional overdose.

Mental Health Support and Suicide Prevention

Most of the overdoses are accidental, but others are triggered by emotional and mental health problems. Addressing the underlying factors, such as depression and suicidal ideation, is life-saving. In case of a possible risk to a person you know, contact a specialist in mental health.

Learn More About Overdose Prevention

Protect yourself and your family by understanding how to safely store medications, recognize overdose symptoms, and seek support. 

Contact us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance to learn how we can help you prevent poisoning and overdose in your home. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands.

Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313

Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

Can poisoning or overdose be reversed?

Yes, many can be reversed with quick medical treatment, like naloxone for opioid overdoses.

How can I prevent accidental poisoning?

Store chemicals and medications safely, and dispose of unused items properly.

What is naloxone, and how does it work?

Naloxone reverses opioid overdoses by blocking the effects of opioids on the brain, especially slowing breathing.

Are all overdoses intentional?

Not all; many overdoses are accidental, especially with medications or household chemicals.

What are the signs of overdose?

Symptoms include unconsciousness, slow breathing, confusion, and seizures. Seek immediate medical help.

How can poisoning be prevented?

Properly store hazardous substances and educate others about their risks.

Does ER of Lufkin treat poisoning and overdose?

Yes, the ER of Lufkin treats poisoning and overdose. ER of Lufkin is equipped to treat both poisoning and overdose cases.

title.rendered: Gastrointestinal Care: Comprehensive Insights for Maintaining Digestive Health

content.raw:
The health of the gastrointestinal or GI system is quite significant to our general health. Our food gets into the digestive system, which breaks down the food into portions that can be utilized, and the by-products are removed. This influences our physical activity and our mental processing. Gastrointestinal disorders like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), Crohn's disease, and food poisoning are common but often misunderstood. Understanding what GI health is, identifying the signs in time, and understanding how to maintain a healthy digestive system are all key to a full and active life. In this blog, we are going to discuss the importance of gut care, common disorders, symptoms to keep an eye on, and simple measures that can be taken to maintain good digestion. This guide will provide you with helpful ideas whether you are currently facing a digestive problem or simply want to be proactive regarding your health.

What is Gastrointestinal Health and Why Is It So Important?

Our gastrointestinal system is far more than just our stomach and intestines; it encompasses the entire digestive process, starting from the mouth to the anus. This system is responsible for breaking down food, absorbing nutrients, and expelling waste. Its proper function is essential for our physical health, immune system, and mental well-being.
  • The Importance of a Healthy Gut: The gut is more than a food eater. It benefits our immune system, our mood, and even our thinking. A normal GI system can enhance digestion, provide energy, and reduce body inflammation.
  • The Gut-Brain Connection: Research indicates that gut bacteria are highly significant to mental health. Gut health may worsen such issues as anxiety, depression, and stress. This indicates the importance of GI care.

Common Gastrointestinal Disorders

Gastrointestinal disorders are different. Their signs may be slight or very painful. Below, we’ll explore some of the most common GI issues, their symptoms, and their treatments.

Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)

According to NIH, IBS is considered to be one of the most widespread GI disorders, and it affects millions of people worldwide. It presents symptoms like stomach pain, fullness, diarrhea, and constipation. IBS is painful, though it does not necessarily damage the intestines.
  • Symptoms of IBS: Abdominal pain, bloating, alternating constipation and diarrhea.
  • Treatment for IBS: The symptoms can be improved with decreasing stress, increasing the fibrous content of the diet, and prescribing medication like antispasmodics, laxatives, or anti-diarrhea agents.

Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)

According to the CDC, IBD has two primary conditions, which are Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. The result of these is inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract in the long term. Both may have a terrible impact on the life of a person and require constant attention.
  • Symptoms of IBD: Persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, blood in stool, and fatigue.
  • Treatment for IBD: Medications to reduce inflammation, immune system suppressors, and, in some cases, surgery may be necessary to remove damaged parts of the intestine.

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)

GERD occurs when stomach acid tends to leak into the esophagus. This leaves the heartburn and at times food returning up. It is also very painful and can destroy the lining of the food pipe unless treated.
  • Symptoms of GERD: Chronic heartburn, difficulty swallowing, chest pain, regurgitation of food.
  • Treatment for GERD: It can be treated by modifying habits such as avoiding food triggers, losing weight, and taking anti-acid medication. Surgery may be required in extreme cases.

Food Poisoning: A Common but Often Preventable Gastrointestinal Issue

According to Medline, food poisoning is a common GI disorder caused by consuming contaminated food or beverages. The most common culprits are bacteria, viruses, or parasites that invade the digestive system and cause a range of symptoms.
  • Symptoms of Food Poisoning: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and sometimes fever. These normally appear several hours after consuming the spoiled food.
  • Treatment for Food Poisoning: Most cases resolve on their own with rest and hydration. However, if symptoms are severe or prolonged, or if you experience signs of dehydration, medical attention should be sought.

Appendicitis: A Life-Threatening Emergency

According to Medline, appendicitis is the inflammation of the appendix, a small organ located near the large intestine. It’s a medical emergency that requires immediate attention. If left untreated, it can lead to a ruptured appendix, which can be fatal.
  • Symptoms of Appendicitis: Severe pain in the lower right side of the abdomen, nausea, vomiting, fever, and loss of appetite.
  • Treatment for Appendicitis: Appendicitis is typically treated with surgery to remove the appendix (appendectomy). Antibiotics may also be administered before and after the surgery to prevent infection.

Understanding Symptoms of Gastrointestinal Disorders

Recognizing symptoms early can help in seeking timely treatment and avoiding long-term complications. Below are common GI symptoms that should not be ignored:

Abdominal Pain and Discomfort

Abdominal pain is a hallmark symptom of many gastrointestinal conditions, including IBS, IBD, and food poisoning. The pain can vary in intensity, location, and duration, and may be accompanied by bloating or changes in bowel movements.

Bloating and Excess Gas

Bloating and excessive gas are common in gastrointestinal disorders like IBS and food intolerance. These symptoms can lead to discomfort, and understanding the causes can help in managing them effectively.

Changes in Bowel Movements

Changes in bowel habits, such as diarrhea, constipation, or blood in the stool, can be symptoms of conditions like IBS, IBD, or infections. Monitoring these changes is important for diagnosing underlying issues.

Nausea and Vomiting

Frequent nausea or vomiting, especially if severe or prolonged, may signal food poisoning, GERD, or more serious GI conditions like appendicitis or IBD. Immediate medical consultation is recommended in such cases.

Unexplained Weight Loss or Fatigue

Unexplained weight loss, coupled with fatigue, can indicate a more serious GI disorder, such as Crohn’s disease, IBD, or cancer. It’s important to seek medical attention if these symptoms are present.

Maintaining a Healthy Gastrointestinal System

Keeping your gastrointestinal system in optimal condition is vital for overall health. Here are some practical tips to help maintain a healthy gut:

The Role of a Balanced Diet

A fiber-rich diet, including fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, promotes healthy digestion and helps prevent constipation. Avoiding processed foods, excessive sugar, and spicy foods can reduce inflammation and prevent flare-ups of conditions like IBS and GERD.

Hydration and Digestion

Drinking plenty of water aids in digestion and helps soften stool, preventing constipation. Proper hydration is essential for maintaining a healthy digestive system.

Stress Management

Chronic stress can worsen conditions like IBS, GERD, and IBD. Incorporating relaxation techniques such as yoga, meditation, or deep breathing exercises into your daily routine can significantly improve gut health.

Probiotics and Gut Health

Probiotics, beneficial bacteria found in yogurt, kefir, and fermented foods, can support a healthy gut microbiome. They help balance gut bacteria, enhance digestion, and boost immune function.

When Should You Seek Medical Help?

While occasional stomach discomfort is common, some symptoms indicate the need for medical attention. These include:
  • Severe or persistent abdominal pain
  • Blood in the stool or vomit
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Chronic diarrhea or constipation
  • Difficulty swallowing or persistent heartburn
If any of these symptoms occur, it’s important to seek medical help for proper diagnosis and treatment.

Prioritize Your Digestive Health Today

If you’re experiencing gastrointestinal disorder symptoms or simply want to learn how to keep your digestive system in top shape, don’t wait. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential for managing symptoms and preventing further complications. Contact the ER of Lufkin today to schedule an appointment with one of our GI specialists. Your digestive health matters, and we’re here to help you feel your best. Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What are the symptoms of IBS?

IBS symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel movements, such as diarrhea or constipation.

How is IBD different from IBS?

IBD (Inflammatory Bowel Disease) causes chronic inflammation in the digestive tract, while IBS is a functional disorder that affects bowel movements and causes discomfort but doesn’t lead to permanent damage.

Can stress worsen gastrointestinal disorders?

Yes, stress can trigger or worsen conditions like IBS, GERD, and IBD, making stress management a key part of treatment.

What is the best diet for a healthy digestive system?

A diet rich in fiber, fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins can support healthy digestion and help prevent many gastrointestinal disorders.

When should I see a doctor for gastrointestinal symptoms?

If you experience severe abdominal pain, blood in your stool or vomit, unexplained weight loss, or persistent nausea and vomiting, it’s important to consult a doctor.

Can food poisoning cause long-term damage?

Most cases of food poisoning are self-limiting, but in severe cases, they can cause long-term damage to the intestines or lead to complications like dehydration.

Does ER of Lufkin treat Gastrointestinal disorders?

Yes, ER of Lufkin treats Gastrointestinal disorders. The facility offers diagnostic and treatment options for various GI conditions.

title.raw: Urinary & Kidney Emergencies: Fast Answers When Minutes Matter
title.rendered: Urinary & Kidney Emergencies: Fast Answers When Minutes Matter

content.raw:
Problems with the urinary system or kidneys don’t always have clear or strong symptoms. Aching pain on one side, a fever with burning urine, or all of a sudden pink or tea colored urine may be a sign of something that may escalate rapidly and cause kidney disease or sepsis by not telling you.  This guide converts expert recommendations that are reliable and government-approved into a language easily understandable by patients and families. We would like to make people see the warning signs, as well as to understand when they have to go to the ER, and what will happen during examinations and treatment.

What counts as a urinary or kidney emergency?

Not all UTI problems are urgent. However, some matters and problems require attention today, which are frequently seen in the emergency room. Go now (ER or 911) if any of the following apply:
  • According to NIDDK, crampy and very strong pain in your side or back, which extends to the lower belly or the groin (typical of stones).
  • According to the CDC, fever and sore throat, urgent, frequent urination, and side or back pain (kidney infection).
  • NIDDK states that blood in the urine is seen- pink, red, brown, or tea (never ignore it).
  • MedlinePlus states that the Inability to urinate (acute urinary retention) or a drastic drop in urine output.
  • According to MedlinePlus, relentless vomiting, dehydration, confusion, or lethargy with urinary complaints include acute kidney injury. 
  • Recent abdominal, back, or pelvic trauma with urinary symptoms.
Why the urgency? Stones, constriction, or an enlarged prostate may create obstructions that are likely to cause the kidneys to be destroyed within a very short time. Sepsis may occur as a result of infections. Fluids and electrolytes may be disturbed by acute kidney injury.

Common kidney emergency scenarios (and how they show up)

Kidney stones (renal colic)

What it feels like: According to NIDDK, the pain is extremely intense on the side or flank, and it occurs in waves. It could be followed by nausea or vomiting. The urine could be pink or red. Why it’s urgent sometimes: According to NIDDK, when the flow of urine is blocked by stones, accompanied by fever, or associated with vomiting, dehydration, one kidney, or visible blood, immediate medical care is required.

Kidney infection (pyelonephritis)

What it feels like: CDC reports that it is accompanied by a fever, chills, pain in the back or sides, and issues in the urine that include burning, urgent urination, and frequent urination. Urgent-care consultation in case of them. Why it’s urgent: CDC states that the infection may be transmitted to the blood (sepsis). All emergency departments usually prescribe fluids and antibiotics.

Acute urinary retention

What it feels like: Painful inability to urinate, lower abdominal pressure, or a striking drop in urine output. Why it’s urgent: Backed-up urine can damage the bladder and kidneys; immediate catheterization may be required.

Blood in the urine (hematuria)

What it looks like: Pink, red, or tea-colored urine. Evaluation is recommended even if it stops. NIDDK When to go now: If hematuria appears with severe pain, fever, trauma, clots, or lightheadedness. NIDDK

Obstructive uropathy/hydronephrosis

What it is: According to  MedlinePlus, a blockage anywhere along the urinary tract that slows or stops urine flow (stone, tumor, stricture, severe BPH). Why urgent: Prolonged obstruction can permanently reduce kidney function; timely decompression is crucial.

Trauma-related urinary injuries

When to worry: After crashes, falls, or sports injuries, watch for flank/abdominal pain, swelling, visible blood in urine, pelvic fractures, or difficulty urinating. 

Acute kidney injury (AKI)

What it is: According to MedlinePlus, a rapid drop in kidney function over hours to days; causes include dehydration, sepsis, obstruction, and medications.  Why it’s dangerous: AKI can cause life-threatening electrolyte issues (e.g., hyperkalemia) and fluid overload; urgent assessment is warranted.

What happens during urgent evaluation

Focused history & red flags

Your clinician will ask about pain pattern, fever/chills, urinary symptoms, urine color, nausea/vomiting, hydration, recent catheter use, meds, pregnancy status, and whether you have a single kidney or a transplant.

Physical exam

Vitals, hydration status, costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness, abdominal/suprapubic exam.

Tests most people get

  • Urinalysis and urine culture (infection, blood, crystals)
  • Blood tests (CBC, BMP) to assess infection, kidney function, and electrolytes
  • Imaging based on clues:
Ultrasound (hydronephrosis, pregnancy) and MR urography when appropriate.

Treatment pathways (the short version)

Kidney infection

  • ED priorities: Fluids, early antibiotics, fever/ pain control.
  • Admission considerations: Vomiting/dehydration, pregnancy, severe illness, immunocompromise.

Stones / renal colic

  • NIDDK states that Analgesia & antiemetics, hydration, urine straining, alpha-blockers may be considered for certain stones; urology consult for large stones, obstruction with infection, solitary kidney, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, or rising creatinine. 

Urinary retention

  • Immediate bladder decompression and evaluation for infection, meds, BPH, or neurologic causes.

Hematuria

  • According to NIDDK, stabilize if heavy bleeding or clots occur; determine the source and risk-stratify for imaging or cystoscopy.

Trauma

  • Follow trauma protocols with early imaging and urology involvement.

Catheter-associated risks (CAUTI)

  • According to the CDC, use catheters only when necessary; follow prevention basics: Hospitals track CAUTI with NHSN

When to call 911 vs urgent care vs same-day clinic

Call 911 or go to the ER now if you have:
  • Severe flank/side pain with fever or vomiting
  • Inability to urinate
  • Visible blood in urine with lightheadedness, clots, or significant pain.
  • Recent trauma to your abdomen, back, or pelvis and urinary symptoms.
  • Signs of sepsis: fever, chills, confusion, fast breathing/heart rate.
Seek same-day urgent evaluation if you have:
  • New visible blood in urine without instability.
  • Moderate stone-like pain that is manageable but persistent. 
  • Painful urination with fever or back pain developing.
  • Worsening urinary symptoms despite home care.

Talking to patients about prevention (brief and practical)

  • Hydration: Aim for pale-yellow urine unless medically restricted.
  • Prompt treatment of UTIs: Don’t “wait it out,” especially with fever or back pain.
  • Catheter care: Use only when necessary
  • Stone risk: Discuss diet and follow-up after the first stone.
  • Follow-through on hematuria: Even if bleeding stops, evaluation matters.

Special situations to handle with extra care

  • Pregnancy: According to the CDC, the lower threshold for imaging (ultrasound preferred) and inpatient antibiotics for kidney infections.
  • Older adults / BPH: Higher risk of retention and atypical infection presentations; “I can’t urinate” is an emergency.
  • Single kidney or transplant: Obstruction/infection can threaten the limited renal reserve, escalating early.
  • Immunocompromised patients: Faster progression and more severe complications are possible.

Worried about a urinary or kidney emergency? 

Don’t wait. If you have severe pain, fever with urinary symptoms, visible blood in your urine, can’t urinate, or you’re getting sicker. Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What symptoms mean that a urinary problem is an emergency?

Severe side/flank pain, fever with urinary symptoms, visible blood in urine, inability to urinate, or persistent vomiting. 

Is it a kidney stone or a kidney infection?

Problems with the urinary system or kidneys don’t always have clear or strong symptoms. Aching pain on one side, a fever with burning urine, or all of a sudden pink or tea colored urine may be a sign of something that may escalate rapidly and cause kidney disease or sepsis by not telling you. 

This guide converts expert recommendations that are reliable and government-approved into a language easily understandable by patients and families. We would like to make people see the warning signs, as well as to understand when they have to go to the ER, and what will happen during examinations and treatment.

What counts as a urinary or kidney emergency?

Not all UTI problems are urgent. However, some matters and problems require attention today, which are frequently seen in the emergency room.

Go now (ER or 911) if any of the following apply:

  • According to NIDDK, crampy and very strong pain in your side or back, which extends to the lower belly or the groin (typical of stones).
  • According to the CDC, fever and sore throat, urgent, frequent urination, and side or back pain (kidney infection).
  • NIDDK states that blood in the urine is seen- pink, red, brown, or tea (never ignore it).
  • MedlinePlus states that the Inability to urinate (acute urinary retention) or a drastic drop in urine output.
  • According to MedlinePlus, relentless vomiting, dehydration, confusion, or lethargy with urinary complaints include acute kidney injury. 
  • Recent abdominal, back, or pelvic trauma with urinary symptoms.

Why the urgency? Stones, constriction, or an enlarged prostate may create obstructions that are likely to cause the kidneys to be destroyed within a very short time. Sepsis may occur as a result of infections. Fluids and electrolytes may be disturbed by acute kidney injury.

Common kidney emergency scenarios (and how they show up)

Kidney stones (renal colic)

What it feels like: According to NIDDK, the pain is extremely intense on the side or flank, and it occurs in waves. It could be followed by nausea or vomiting. The urine could be pink or red.

Why it’s urgent sometimes: According to NIDDK, when the flow of urine is blocked by stones, accompanied by fever, or associated with vomiting, dehydration, one kidney, or visible blood, immediate medical care is required.

Kidney infection (pyelonephritis)

What it feels like: CDC reports that it is accompanied by a fever, chills, pain in the back or sides, and issues in the urine that include burning, urgent urination, and frequent urination. Urgent-care consultation in case of them.

Why it’s urgent: CDC states that the infection may be transmitted to the blood (sepsis). All emergency departments usually prescribe fluids and antibiotics.

Acute urinary retention

What it feels like: Painful inability to urinate, lower abdominal pressure, or a striking drop in urine output.

Why it’s urgent: Backed-up urine can damage the bladder and kidneys; immediate catheterization may be required.

Blood in the urine (hematuria)

What it looks like: Pink, red, or tea-colored urine. Evaluation is recommended even if it stops. NIDDK

When to go now: If hematuria appears with severe pain, fever, trauma, clots, or lightheadedness. NIDDK

Obstructive uropathy/hydronephrosis

What it is: According to  MedlinePlus, a blockage anywhere along the urinary tract that slows or stops urine flow (stone, tumor, stricture, severe BPH).

Why urgent: Prolonged obstruction can permanently reduce kidney function; timely decompression is crucial.

Trauma-related urinary injuries

When to worry: After crashes, falls, or sports injuries, watch for flank/abdominal pain, swelling, visible blood in urine, pelvic fractures, or difficulty urinating. 

Acute kidney injury (AKI)

What it is: According to MedlinePlus, a rapid drop in kidney function over hours to days; causes include dehydration, sepsis, obstruction, and medications. 

Why it’s dangerous: AKI can cause life-threatening electrolyte issues (e.g., hyperkalemia) and fluid overload; urgent assessment is warranted.

What happens during urgent evaluation

Focused history & red flags

Your clinician will ask about pain pattern, fever/chills, urinary symptoms, urine color, nausea/vomiting, hydration, recent catheter use, meds, pregnancy status, and whether you have a single kidney or a transplant.

Physical exam

Vitals, hydration status, costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness, abdominal/suprapubic exam.

Tests most people get

  • Urinalysis and urine culture (infection, blood, crystals)
  • Blood tests (CBC, BMP) to assess infection, kidney function, and electrolytes
  • Imaging based on clues:

Ultrasound (hydronephrosis, pregnancy) and MR urography when appropriate.

Treatment pathways (the short version)

Kidney infection

  • ED priorities: Fluids, early antibiotics, fever/ pain control.
  • Admission considerations: Vomiting/dehydration, pregnancy, severe illness, immunocompromise.

Stones / renal colic

  • NIDDK states that Analgesia & antiemetics, hydration, urine straining, alpha-blockers may be considered for certain stones; urology consult for large stones, obstruction with infection, solitary kidney, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, or rising creatinine. 

Urinary retention

  • Immediate bladder decompression and evaluation for infection, meds, BPH, or neurologic causes.

Hematuria

  • According to NIDDK, stabilize if heavy bleeding or clots occur; determine the source and risk-stratify for imaging or cystoscopy.

Trauma

  • Follow trauma protocols with early imaging and urology involvement.

Catheter-associated risks (CAUTI)

  • According to the CDC, use catheters only when necessary; follow prevention basics: Hospitals track CAUTI with NHSN

When to call 911 vs urgent care vs same-day clinic

Call 911 or go to the ER now if you have:

  • Severe flank/side pain with fever or vomiting
  • Inability to urinate
  • Visible blood in urine with lightheadedness, clots, or significant pain.
  • Recent trauma to your abdomen, back, or pelvis and urinary symptoms.
  • Signs of sepsis: fever, chills, confusion, fast breathing/heart rate.

Seek same-day urgent evaluation if you have:

  • New visible blood in urine without instability.
  • Moderate stone-like pain that is manageable but persistent. 
  • Painful urination with fever or back pain developing.
  • Worsening urinary symptoms despite home care.

Talking to patients about prevention (brief and practical)

  • Hydration: Aim for pale-yellow urine unless medically restricted.
  • Prompt treatment of UTIs: Don’t “wait it out,” especially with fever or back pain.
  • Catheter care: Use only when necessary
  • Stone risk: Discuss diet and follow-up after the first stone.
  • Follow-through on hematuria: Even if bleeding stops, evaluation matters.

  • Pregnancy: According to the CDC, the lower threshold for imaging (ultrasound preferred) and inpatient antibiotics for kidney infections.
  • Older adults / BPH: Higher risk of retention and atypical infection presentations; “I can’t urinate” is an emergency.
  • Single kidney or transplant: Obstruction/infection can threaten the limited renal reserve, escalating early.
  • Immunocompromised patients: Faster progression and more severe complications are possible.

Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands.
