title.raw: Respiratory Illnesses: Symptoms, Testing, Prevention, and When to Seek Care
title.rendered: Respiratory Illnesses: Symptoms, Testing, Prevention, and When to Seek Care

content.raw:
Among the most frequent causes of seeking medical assistance, breathing issues should be mentioned. They peak during fall and winter, following travel, and when there is low-quality air. CDC states respiratory illness refers to common colds and other severe infections, such as influenza and pneumonia.  Such diseases include chronic airway diseases like asthma and COPD. Understanding the modes of spreading these illnesses, their risk factor, and what prevention is effective will help you safeguard yourself and your loved ones.

What counts as a “respiratory illness”? (Upper vs. lower; acute vs. chronic)

Upper respiratory tract conditions involve the throat, sinuses, and nose- this includes colds, laryngitis, pharyngitis, and sinusitis. Lower respiratory tract disorders affect the airways and lungs - they include acute bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia. NCBI maintains that lower-tract infections can tend to be more shortness-limiting and more severe, particularly in the elderly as well as in individuals with chronic illnesses. Respiratory illnesses can also be grouped by time course:
  • Acute: colds, influenza, COVID-19, RSV, acute bronchitis, pneumonia.
  • Chronic: According to NIH, asthma, COPD, and bronchiectasis can last and can increase with infections or irritants, for a quick primer on acute bronchitis (short-term airway inflammation with cough).

Common respiratory illnesses (skimmable quick guides)

Colds (Viral Upper Respiratory Infection)

Coughing, sore throats, and runny or stuffy noses are common symptoms of colds. The majority don't need antibiotics and are self-sustainable. The CDC states that testing for flu, COVID-19, or RSV may be beneficial if it could change treatment for people at high risk or in cases when symptoms are severe or chronic.

Influenza (Flu)

According to the CDC and Key Facts About Seasonal Flu Vaccine, flu may be mild to severe, and in some cases, it results in hospitalization or even death. The most effective preventive measure is yearly vaccination, preferably since the age of six, although there are rare exceptions, and it minimizes the chances of hospitalization and mortality.

COVID-19

According to the CDC, respiratory waves of COVID-19 continue to season. There is an improvement in terms of testing and treatment options, including antivirals for qualified people. Consult your local information on isolation, testing when, and vaccination.

RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus)

According to the CDC, RSV is frequently associated with a cold, and it is one of the leading causes of infant hospitalization and may be severe in older adults. The agency includes the risk factors, testing, and prevention, such as the immunization of eligible groups by the ACIP.

Acute bronchitis

According to NIH, a cough, which is typically viral, may continue for weeks even after you feel better overall. Unless your doctor finds a bacterial cause or another illness, antibiotics are rarely required. If your cough drags on for weeks, our guide to a persistent cough covers when it needs medical attention. 

Pneumonia

MedlinePlus states that  Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs, which is filled with fluid or pus in the air sacs. The most common symptoms that should be considered as warning signs are fever, dyspnea, chest pain, which becomes more severe during deep breathing, and a productive cough, particularly in elderly individuals or those with chronic health problems.

Asthma & COPD (chronic airway diseases)

According to NIH, Asthma often features episodic wheeze and variable airflow, with triggers such as exercise, allergens, or viruses; COPD includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis with progressive shortness of breath and chronic cough/sputum, usually in current or former smokers. 

How these illnesses spread and what raises risk

According to the CDC, respiratory viral infections are transmitted by the droplet and aerosol methods in the form of coughing, sneezing, speaking, and being close together. The steps to prevention are based on vaccination, hand hygiene, better indoor air and ventilation, and sick leave. Who’s at higher risk? Children under the age of 5 years and elderly individuals, asthmatic and COPD patients, individuals with heart or kidney disease, diabetes, pregnant and immunocompromised patients, and individuals who are exposed to irritants regularly (smoke, dust, pollution) or spend a lot of time in crowded indoor environments. Occupational and environmental exposures matter. According to NIOSH and OSHA, for information on workplace hazards and precautions, see 29 CFR 1910.134. The EPA and AirNow provide doable exposure-reduction and indoor-air strategies for days with smoke and poor air quality. Rural East Texas has its own exposure risk: our hantavirus guide covers the breathing symptoms that can follow cleaning rodent-infested spaces. 

Symptoms: what’s typical and what’s a red flag

Symptoms in the upper-airway (preeminent with colds): runny nose, stuffy nose, sore throat, sinus pressure, cough with mild intensity, fatigue. Lower-airway symptoms (more alarming): dyspnea, chest tightness, wheezing, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, increasing fever or chills. According to NIH, these are patterns that can be used to differentiate between acute bronchitis (the symptoms are typically post-viral cough and low-grade fever) and pneumonia (elevated fever, SOB, chest discomfort). Attend to an emergency or urgent care as soon as possible in case you or someone you love has:
  • severe shortness of breath
  • lips or face turning blue
  • chest pain or pressure
  • confusion, fainting, or extreme dehydration
  • high fever (≥103 °F / 39.4 °C)
  • coughing up blood
  • or a sudden increase in symptoms of infants, older adults, or individuals with chronic heart/lung disease.

Testing and diagnosis: what to expect

History & exam: clinicians inquire about the onset, contacts (sick, travel, wildfire smoke), seasonality, vaccination history, and comorbidities. They seek breathing effort, oxygen levels, and lung sounds. Point-of-care tests: rapid flu, COVID-19, and RSV tests can specify the diagnosis (e.g., antivirals, isolating vulnerable contacts). Imaging & pulmonary tests: MedlinePlus specifies that a chest X-ray can be requested in case of suspicion of pneumonia. Spirometry determines airflow (asthma/COPD) in cases of chronic or recurrent symptoms. Take your clinician-directed post-pneumonia education and post-care.

Treatment and self-care: what actually helps

Supportive care you can start today According to CDC Hydration, rest, saline nasal rinses, and cleaner indoor air (ventilation/filtration) are simple, effective steps. When sick, stay home to avoid spreading illness, and contact a clinician promptly if you’re in a high-risk group.  Use over-the-counter (OTC) medicines wisely Analgesics/antipyretics (e.g., acetaminophen/ibuprofen) can ease fever and aches. Decongestants/antihistamines may help some symptoms but have age and medical-condition cautions; always follow labels and clinician advice, especially for children and during pregnancy.  Prescription therapies
  • The CDC recommends antivirals against flu, and COVID antivirals when necessary, as most effective when given early after symptom onset. The eligibility is based on timing, risk factors, and medication interactions. Inquire with your clinician about whether you are eligible.
  • NIH states that bronchodilators can be effective in improving asthma and COPD attacks. Steroids can be given for a short term. Long-term control strategies and the use of inhaler technique are also significant.
Home monitoring & “return precautions” CDC states that track fever trends and symptoms; consider a pulse oximeter if recommended by your clinician (especially in high-risk patients). Seek care if symptoms worsen or don’t follow the expected course. 

Prevention that works (vaccines + air + habits)

Everyday prevention (CDC): stay home if sick; wash hands regularly; clean high-touch surfaces; improve indoor air with ventilation/filtration; and consider masking in high-risk settings or during surges. Vaccination
  • Flu: everyone ≥6 months should get a yearly flu vaccine, with rare exceptions; as of 2024–2025, U.S. flu vaccines are trivalent. 
  • RSV: CDC/ACIP outlines immunization options for eligible groups (e.g., certain infants via nirsevimab; older adults via RSV vaccines) and monitors safety. 
  • COVID-19: follow your local and CDC guidance each season (product availability and timing can change). 
Air quality & wildfire smoke On smoky or poor-AQI days, reduce exposure: keep windows closed, run HVAC on recirculate with a clean high-MERV filter, use a portable HEPA cleaner sized for your room, and limit strenuous outdoor activity.  Workplace protections Employers must protect workers from airborne hazards.

Seasonality, surges, and planning ahead

According to the CDC, U.S. flu activity typically peaks in December–February, but it varies; aim to vaccinate before local surges and pay attention to real-time respiratory-virus dashboards and local public-health updates.

Special populations: extra care, extra clarity

  • Infants & children: higher risk from RSV and flu; watch for feeding difficulty, fast breathing, chest retractions, or dehydration—and call promptly if present.
  • Older adults & chronic conditions: prioritize vaccinations and early evaluation for fever/SOB; consider pulse-ox monitoring if advised. 
  • Pregnancy: higher risk for complications from respiratory infections; discuss vaccine timing and safe symptom relief with your clinician.

Breathe Easier: Get Same-Day Respiratory Care 

Breathing shouldn’t feel like a struggle. If you’re dealing with a persistent cough, fever, chest tightness, wheezing, or shortness of breath, the ER of Lufkin can evaluate you quickly, day or night. Our team provides prompt assessment, appropriate testing (as clinically indicated), and treatment plans tailored to your symptoms and risk factors. Contact the ER of Lufkin today to schedule a consultation or book a visit Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What are the most common respiratory illnesses right now?

Seasonal patterns vary, but flu, COVID-19, RSV, and colds are common drivers.

How do I know if my cough is bronchitis or pneumonia?

Bronchitis often follows a cold with a cough that lingers; pneumonia is more likely if you have a fever, shortness of breath, and chest pain. Clinicians may order a chest X-ray. 

When should I go to the ER for breathing problems?

Go now for severe shortness of breath, blue lips/face, chest pain/pressure, confusion/fainting, very high fever (≥103°F/39.4°C), coughing blood, or rapid worsening in infants/older adults/chronic disease.

Do I need a test for flu/COVID/RSV, or can I just rest at home?

Testing helps when results would change care (e.g., antivirals, isolation to protect high-risk contacts). Your clinician can advise based on symptoms and timing. See CDC’s respiratory hub and RSV overview.

What really works to prevent respiratory illnesses?

Vaccination, staying home when sick, hand hygiene, and cleaner indoor air (ventilation/filtration) reduce spread.

When is flu season, and when should I get vaccinated?

U.S. flu activity usually peaks in December–February; vaccinate before local surges. 

How can I protect my lungs during wildfire smoke days?

Keep windows closed, run HVAC on recirculate with a clean high-MERV filter, use a portable HEPA cleaner, and limit outdoor exertion. 

Does ER of Lufkin treat respiratory illnesses?

Yes, the ER of Lufkin treats respiratory illnesses. We’re open 24/7 for urgent breathing concerns, including flu, COVID-19, RSV, acute bronchitis, pneumonia, and asthma/COPD flare-ups.

title.raw: Why Understanding Trauma and Accidents Is Crucial
title.rendered: Why Understanding Trauma and Accidents Is Crucial

content.raw:
Trauma and accidents are the unfortunate side of life, and millions of individuals are victims each year. The physical injuries, but also emotional and psychological wounds, may arise because of a sudden car crash, a fall, or an act of violence. This blog aims to explain the critical nature of trauma and accidents, why it’s essential to address both the physical and emotional impacts, and how you can seek help to heal, whether you or a loved one is experiencing the aftermath of trauma.

What Is Trauma? Understanding Its Impact on Your Life

Defining Trauma: Beyond the Physical

According to APA, trauma is the emotional, psychological, and physical response to a painful experience in a person. Popular triggers include accidents, violence, disasters, and abuse.

Types of Trauma:

  • Acute Trauma: An accident or injury.
  • Chronic Trauma: Repeated or prolonged stress in life, such as living in a violent neighborhood.
  • Complex Trauma: The combined impact of multiple traumatic events, often occurring over a long period, like child abuse or ongoing violence.
Trauma should be viewed as both physical and emotional to deal with the entire range of recovery. Some people portray visible damage, and others possess deep emotional wounds, which are more difficult to detect but prove to be equally damaging.

The Biological and Emotional Impact of Trauma

Trauma not only impacts the mind, but it also affects the body a lot. Because your body responds to stress through the fight-or-flight response that is activated when you experience a traumatic event, your body releases the hormones that allow it to respond to dangerous situations: adrenaline and cortisol. Although this reaction is beneficial in the face of immediate danger, recurring uses may bring in long-term effects, which may be chronic pain, sleeping difficulties, as well as depression of the psyche, such as anxiety or PTSD. If trauma is not appropriately addressed, its long-term effects can compromise both your physical and emotional well-being.

Common Types of Accidents and Their Consequences

Accidental Injuries: A Leading Cause of Death and Disability

Accidental injuries ruin lives and cause death all over the globe. The CDC claims millions of emergency visits each year due to accidents like motor vehicle and fall accidents, as well as drowning.

Types of Accidents:

  • Car Accidents: This is due to the high incidence of injuries, which includes mild concussions to fatal injuries.
  • Falls: Lots of older adults fall quite often and can cause fractures, head injuries, and long-term disability.
  • Workplace Injuries: Some workplaces are more likely to cause accidents that can cause serious bodily injuries, such as in construction and manufacturing.
Accidents are complex to traumatize. It is not just physical injuries to deal with, but sometimes the emotional consequences are too much to handle, particularly for the victims of serious accidents. Statistics: According to the CDC, approximately 200,000 injuries are caused annually in the U.S. alone due to unintentional injuries. These figures only scratch the surface, as many more are injured in accidents annually.

Physical Injuries and Trauma: What Happens to Your Body?

In case of an accident, the body can be seriously harmed. Physical injuries constitute fractures, burns, concussions, and lacerations. The body can respond in a variety of ways, based on the type of injury, yet recovery is crucial to recovery in both body and mind. It is crucial to visit a doctor and ensure medical help as soon as possible to avoid complications and encourage a long-term recovery.

Trauma-Informed Care: Why It Matters

What Is Trauma-Informed Care?

Trauma-informed care is a therapeutic approach that recognizes that widespread trauma may affect people and that physical and spiritual safety are important. The trained providers of this model are aware of the behaviors as a consequence of trauma and ensure that care is non-threatening and gentle. The key principles include:
  • Safety: Ensuring that the patient feels physically and emotionally safe.
  • Trustworthiness: Building trust by providing transparent care processes.
  • Empowerment: Encouraging the patient’s participation in decisions about their care.
Trauma-informed care is essential because it acknowledges that trauma impacts every person differently, and their healing process will be unique.

How Healthcare Providers Can Help You Recover

Both the physical injuries of the accidents and the emotional harm of the trauma have to be treated by healthcare providers. SAMHSA says counseling, support groups, or trauma-focused therapy can actually help in saving a life. Trauma centers are specialized Medicare centers that offer whole-person care, comprising both body and mind.

The Emotional and Psychological Effects of Accidents and Trauma

Mental Health Impacts of Trauma and Accidents

The traumatic effects psychologically have a lasting effect on the physical injuries. It frequently results in conditions that include:
  • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD): A common condition for those who have been involved in traumatic accidents.
  • Anxiety: Trauma survivors often experience heightened fear, panic, and anxiety.
  • Depression: The emotional aftermath of trauma can lead to feelings of hopelessness or worthlessness.
It is crucial to realize that trauma is not only in your head to heal it. It transforms the way you think, experience, and relate to other people.

Supporting Loved Ones Through Trauma

When a loved one is experiencing trauma, be patient, open, and encouraging to seek help. Hear them out; they need you, and listening is the best way to support them in the process of recovery.

Prevention and Awareness: Reducing the Risk of Trauma and Accidents

Simple Ways to Prevent Accidents

Education is the first step towards accident prevention. The simplest form of safety precautions may include wearing seat belts, using safety gear at the workplace, and reducing slips and falls that may result in injuries at home. Other tips include:
  • Driving Safely: Always use your seatbelt and avoid distractions.
  • Workplace Safety: Follow safety protocols and report hazards.
  • Home Safety: Use handrails, ensure good lighting, and clean up spills immediately.

Recognizing Early Signs of Trauma

Recognizing the early signs of trauma is essential for getting the right help. Symptoms might include:
  • Unexplained physical complaints (e.g., chronic pain, headaches)
  • Flashbacks or nightmares
  • Withdrawal from social interactions
Early recognition and intervention can help reduce the severity of trauma and prevent long-term mental health issues.

What to Do After an Accident: Immediate Steps to Take

First Aid: Immediate Care to Prevent Long-Term Damage

In the event of an accident, providing immediate first aid is critical. Basic first aid steps include:
  • Stop the Bleeding: Apply pressure to wounds.
  • Check for Breathing: If the person is unconscious, check for normal breathing and start CPR if needed.
  • Keep Calm and Seek Help: Call 911 immediately for professional medical assistance.
These actions can help minimize the risk of further injury and keep the person stable until help arrives.

Seeking Professional Help After Trauma

Professional assistance is vital in case such a traumatic event occurs to you or someone you care about. According to SAMHSA, professionals can offer physical and emotional treatment that favors healing. Ensure that you contact trauma specialists, therapists, and providers of emergency care.

How to Cope with Trauma: Recovery and Healing

Recovery: What to Expect

Trauma will take a long time to heal. After physical wounds, it might take weeks or months to recover, but what can take a long time to recover are the emotional and psychological wounds. The supportive therapies, self-care, and counseling are all fundamental to the healing. It is important to remember that the process of recovery is not linear; good days will be followed by difficult days. One step at a time will result in the recovery being long-term.

Healing Is Possible: Finding Hope

There is hope for healing, and recovery is entirely possible with the right support. Whether through therapy, medication, or simply connecting with loved ones, everyone’s journey is different, but it’s important to remember that you don’t have to go through it alone.

Take the Next Step Toward Healing

If you or a loved one has been affected by trauma or an accident, don’t wait to seek help. Reach out to the ER of Lufkin, where compassionate, trauma-informed care is available to guide you through your recovery process. Whether you need emergency care, mental health support, or physical therapy, our dedicated team is here to help.  Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What is trauma, and how does it affect my health?

Trauma refers to physical or emotional responses to distressing events like accidents, abuse, or violence.

How can accidents lead to long-term trauma?

Accidents can result in both physical injuries and psychological impacts. 

What are the most common types of accidents that result in trauma?

The most common accidents that result in trauma include car accidents, falls, workplace injuries, sports-related injuries, and physical assaults.

What is trauma-informed care, and why is it important?

Trauma-informed care is an approach that recognizes the widespread impact of trauma and seeks to provide safe, supportive, and understanding care. 

How can I support a loved one who has experienced trauma?

To support a loved one who has experienced trauma, be patient, listen without judgment, and encourage them to seek professional help.

When should I seek medical help after an accident?

You should seek medical help immediately after an accident if you experience serious pain, difficulty breathing, unconsciousness, significant bleeding, or any signs of head or neck injuries.

Can trauma affect children differently from adults?

Yes, trauma can affect children differently. Children may have difficulty expressing their emotions, and trauma can affect their development, behavior, and relationships.

Does ER of Lufkin treat trauma and accidents?

Yes, ER of Lufkin provides comprehensive treatment for trauma and accidents.

title.rendered: Understanding High Fever and Its Impact on Health

content.raw:
High fever may be a terrifying experience either as a person or when attending to another. However, what does it mean, and when must you be concerned with something more serious? A typical symptom of infection is fever. It can get very high and be very problematic. High temperatures are uncomfortable and alarming, which can cause worry if the home remedies are not effective. Although this fever has become a natural body reaction to fighting infection, a high fever should be treated specially. This guide covers the process of treating a high fever, the symptoms that need to be observed, and when and where to seek medical help.

What is a high fever?

A fever is typically a body temperature of  100.4°F (38°C) or higher. It displays that the immune system is attacking an infection. According to the CDC, fever is a common symptom of numerous conditions, as well as a sign of a severe disease.

Fever Classifications:

  • Low-grade: 37.3 to 38.0 °C (99.1 to 100.4 °F)
  • Moderate-grade: 38.1 to 39.0 °C (100.6 to 102.2 °F)
  • High-grade: 39.1 to 41 °C (102.4 to 105.8 F)
  • Hyperthermia: Greater than 41 °C (105.8 °F)
The majority of fevers are treated at home; however, when the fever exceeds or you experience certain effects of stiffness in the neck, a rash, or stomachaches, the case is treated as an emergency.

Causes of High Fever

According to the CDC, there are many causes of high fever, most commonly infections. These can include:
  • Viral infections: Flu, cold, COVID-19, and others.
  • Bacterial infections: Like typhoid fever, pneumonia, and urinary tract infections.
  • Heatstroke: When the body overheats due to prolonged exposure to hot weather or strenuous activity.
  • Medication reactions: Certain medications may cause fever as a side effect.

When Should You Be Concerned About a High Fever?

Warning Signs That High Fever May Be Serious

According to Medline, most fevers are not dangerous, but a high fever, especially if it’s persistent or accompanied by other symptoms, can be a sign of a more serious condition. Here are some warning signs to look out for:
  • Fever that lasts more than three days.
  • Severe headache or neck stiffness.
  • Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath.
  • Rash or unusual spots on the skin.
  • Confusion, delirium, or seizures.
The symptoms might be an indication of a severe infection or condition that requires medical care.

Specific Risk Factors

NIH states that certain people are at greater risk for complications from high fever. This includes:
  • Infants and young children: Their immune systems are still developing, and high fevers can be more dangerous.
  • Elderly individuals: Older adults may not regulate their body temperature as effectively.
  • People with compromised immune systems: Those undergoing chemotherapy or who have chronic illnesses are at increased risk for complications from fever.

How to Care for a High Fever at Home

When to Monitor and When to Seek Medical Help

The high temperature does not even mean that the doctor has to visit him all the time. A simple home remedy can take care of a fever on most occasions. Once the fever lasts for several days or you realize that you experience some of the warning signs described above, then it is time to get some medical help. According to the CDC, monitor the fever regularly with a thermometer. If the fever reaches over 103°F (39.4°C) and does not respond to fever-reducing medications like acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil), seek medical advice.

Home Remedies for Lowering Fever

These are some ways of safe home management of fever:
  1. Hydration: Staying hydrated is crucial. Drink plenty of fluids like water, clear soups, or oral rehydration solutions to prevent dehydration, which can occur during a fever.
  2. Rest: Your body needs energy to fight the infection, so rest is vital for recovery.
  3. Cooling Techniques: Apply a cool compress to your forehead or take a lukewarm bath. Avoid ice-cold baths, as they can cause shivering, which may increase the body’s temperature.
  4. Fever-Reducing Medications: Over-the-counter medications like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help reduce fever. Be sure to follow the dosing instructions carefully.

Medical Interventions for High Fever

When Medical Help is Necessary

When the fever continues for more than 3 days and is not improving with the help of fever reducers, or you are having any severe symptoms stated above, it's time to see a doctor. A high fever may be a warning of a bacterial disease or other condition that needs prescription medications to treat, like antibiotics or anti-viral medications.

Hospital Treatments for High Fever

If the fever is severe or poses a threat to your health, you may need to go to the hospital for further treatment, which can include:
  • IV fluids to rehydrate your body.
  • Cooling treatments, such as ice baths or cold packs.
  • Blood tests are used to determine if a bacterial infection is present.
  • Antibiotics or antivirals, depending on the cause of the fever.

Preventing High Fever and Its Causes

Best Practices to Avoid Fever-Related Illnesses

  1. Good Hygiene: Regular hand washing can prevent the spread of infectious agents.
  2. Stay Up to Date on Vaccinations: Immunizations help prevent certain infections that can cause fever, like the flu or measles.
  3. Avoid Overheating: Dress appropriately for the weather and stay cool to avoid heatstroke.

Keeping Your Immune System Strong

A healthy immune system can fight off infections more effectively, reducing the risk of fever:
  • Eat a balanced diet rich in vitamins and minerals.
  • Exercise regularly to boost overall health.
  • Sleep well, as adequate rest is key to immune function.

Get Immediate Care for High Fever

Worried about a high fever or experiencing concerning symptoms? Don't wait to get the care you need. Contact the ER of Lufkin today to schedule a consultation or book a visit. Our experienced team is here to help you manage fever safely and ensure you get the professional care you deserve. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What is considered a high fever?

A fever is considered high if it exceeds 103°F (39.4°C).

When should I take a fever reducer?

If the fever causes discomfort or reaches 103°F (39.4°C), consider using a fever reducer.

What are some signs of a serious fever?

Warning signs include persistent fever, confusion, trouble breathing, severe headache, or a rash.

How can I lower a high fever naturally?

Drink fluids, rest, and use a cool compress or lukewarm bath to lower fever.

When should I seek medical attention for a fever?

Seek medical help if the fever lasts more than 3 days, is unresponsive to medications, or if severe symptoms appear.

Can a fever be dangerous?

Yes, if left untreated, a high fever can lead to serious complications like dehydration or brain damage.

How can I prevent a high fever?

Practice good hygiene, stay hydrated, and avoid exposure to infections.

Does ER of Lufkin treat high fever?

Yes, the ER of Lufkin treats high fever. Our experienced medical team is equipped to provide immediate care and manage high fevers effectively, ensuring your health and safety.

Once the fever lasts for several days or you realize that you experience some of the warning signs described above, then it is time to get some medical help.

According to the CDC, monitor the fever regularly with a thermometer. If the fever reaches over 103°F (39.4°C) and does not respond to fever-reducing medications like acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil), seek medical advice.

Home Remedies for Lowering Fever

These are some ways of safe home management of fever:

  1. Hydration: Staying hydrated is crucial. Drink plenty of fluids like water, clear soups, or oral rehydration solutions to prevent dehydration, which can occur during a fever.
  2. Rest: Your body needs energy to fight the infection, so rest is vital for recovery.
  3. Cooling Techniques: Apply a cool compress to your forehead or take a lukewarm bath. Avoid ice-cold baths, as they can cause shivering, which may increase the body’s temperature.
  4. Fever-Reducing Medications: Over-the-counter medications like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help reduce fever. Be sure to follow the dosing instructions carefully.

Medical Interventions for High Fever

When Medical Help is Necessary

When the fever continues for more than 3 days and is not improving with the help of fever reducers, or you are having any severe symptoms stated above, it’s time to see a doctor.

A high fever may be a warning of a bacterial disease or other condition that needs prescription medications to treat, like antibiotics or anti-viral medications.

Hospital Treatments for High Fever

If the fever is severe or poses a threat to your health, you may need to go to the hospital for further treatment, which can include:

  • IV fluids to rehydrate your body.
  • Cooling treatments, such as ice baths or cold packs.
  • Blood tests are used to determine if a bacterial infection is present.
  • Antibiotics or antivirals, depending on the cause of the fever.

Preventing High Fever and Its Causes

Best Practices to Avoid Fever-Related Illnesses

  1. Good Hygiene: Regular hand washing can prevent the spread of infectious agents.
  2. Stay Up to Date on Vaccinations: Immunizations help prevent certain infections that can cause fever, like the flu or measles.
  3. Avoid Overheating: Dress appropriately for the weather and stay cool to avoid heatstroke.

Keeping Your Immune System Strong

A healthy immune system can fight off infections more effectively, reducing the risk of fever:

  • Eat a balanced diet rich in vitamins and minerals.
  • Exercise regularly to boost overall health.
  • Sleep well, as adequate rest is key to immune function.

Get Immediate Care for High Fever

Worried about a high fever or experiencing concerning symptoms? Don’t wait to get the care you need. Contact the ER of Lufkin today to schedule a consultation or book a visit. Our experienced team is here to help you manage fever safely and ensure you get the professional care you deserve.

Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313

Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

What is considered a high fever?

A fever is considered high if it exceeds 103°F (39.4°C).

When should I take a fever reducer?

If the fever causes discomfort or reaches 103°F (39.4°C), consider using a fever reducer.

What are some signs of a serious fever?

Warning signs include persistent fever, confusion, trouble breathing, severe headache, or a rash.

How can I lower a high fever naturally?

Drink fluids, rest, and use a cool compress or lukewarm bath to lower fever.

When should I seek medical attention for a fever?

Seek medical help if the fever lasts more than 3 days, is unresponsive to medications, or if severe symptoms appear.

Can a fever be dangerous?

Yes, if left untreated, a high fever can lead to serious complications like dehydration or brain damage.

How can I prevent a high fever?

Practice good hygiene, stay hydrated, and avoid exposure to infections.

Yes, the ER of Lufkin treats high fever. Our experienced medical team is equipped to provide immediate care and manage high fevers effectively, ensuring your health and safety.

title.rendered: Animal Bites: First Aid, Infection Signs, and When to Get Emergency Care

content.raw:
An animal bite can range from barely-broken skin to a deep puncture wound that needs surgery. Knowing how to clean a bite, when it can wait until morning, and when it needs the ER can prevent serious infection, rabies exposure, and tetanus complications.

This guide covers first aid for dog and cat bites, infection warning signs, when bites need emergency care, and the most common bite-related diseases including rabies, tetanus, cat scratch fever, and capnocytophaga.

What Are Animal Bites?

Animal bites are wounds caused by an animal's teeth or claws breaking the skin. The MedlinePlus animal bites guide notes that even a small bite can introduce bacteria deep into tissue, where the body has trouble fighting infection.

Dogs cause the majority of bite injuries in the United States. Cats cause fewer bites, but cat bites are deeper and more likely to become infected because cat teeth create narrow puncture wounds that trap bacteria.

Wild animal bites from raccoons, skunks, bats, and foxes carry the additional concern of rabies. Bites from livestock or exotic pets can carry less-common but serious infections.

The risk a bite poses depends on the animal, the bite location, the depth, and how quickly first aid begins.

How Animal Bites Occur: Common Scenarios

Domestic Animal Bites

Most bites in the United States come from dogs and cats kept as pets. Children are bitten more often than adults, and most childhood bites involve the face or hands. Familiar dogs (the family pet, neighbor's dog) cause more bites than stray dogs.

Wild Animal Bites

Encounters with raccoons, skunks, bats, foxes, and coyotes can lead to bites or scratches. Bats are a special concern: a small bat scratch may not be felt or remembered, but bat exposure is the most common cause of human rabies in the United States.

Livestock and Farm Animal Bites

Horses, cattle, pigs, and goats can deliver crushing bites due to their size and strength. These bites often need surgical evaluation even when the skin damage looks limited.

The Risks of Animal Bites: When to Worry

Animal bites carry three main risks: infection, tetanus, and rabies.

Infection Risk

According to Mayo Clinic, prompt wound care matters. Starting first aid within 6 hours of the bite reduces infection risk dramatically. Wounds left untreated for longer become much more likely to become infected.

Cat bites have the highest infection rate. Around 50 percent of cat bites become infected because cat teeth create deep, narrow puncture wounds that seal at the surface and trap bacteria below.

Signs of Infection

Watch for these warning signs in the days after a bite:

  • Increasing redness, swelling, or warmth around the bite
  • Pus or yellow drainage from the wound
  • Red streaks extending up the limb from the bite site
  • Fever or chills
  • Increasing pain instead of gradual improvement
  • Sudden confusion, especially in older adults

Bite-related infections can progress to cellulitis or abscess and, in severe cases, sepsis. Get evaluated at the first sign of infection.

What to Do After an Animal Bite: First Aid

Start first aid immediately, ideally within the first hour and definitely within 6 hours. The basic steps are the same for most bites, with important differences between dog and cat bites.

Step-by-Step First Aid

  1. Stop bleeding with firm direct pressure using a clean cloth.
  2. Wash the wound with mild soap and warm running water for at least 5 minutes. This is the single most important step.
  3. Apply an antibiotic ointment if you have one.
  4. Cover with a sterile bandage and change it daily.
  5. Watch for infection signs over the next 24 to 72 hours.

Dog Bites

Dog bites tend to cause lacerations and crushing injuries because of jaw strength. Visible damage often understates the deeper tissue injury. Bites that bleed heavily or expose tissue beneath the skin need ER evaluation.

Cat Bites

Cat bites look small but go deep. Because cat teeth create narrow puncture wounds, they share many of the same concerns as stepping on a nail. Bacteria get trapped below the surface where flushing is hard.

Cat bites on the hand, especially over a joint, almost always need professional evaluation and antibiotics.

Prevention: How to Avoid Animal Bites

Most bites happen during routine interactions, not random attacks. A few habits reduce risk:

  • Avoid approaching unfamiliar dogs or cats
  • Never disturb an animal that is eating, sleeping, or caring for young
  • Avoid wild animals, especially those acting unusually tame or aggressive
  • Keep pet vaccinations current, especially rabies
  • Spay or neuter pets to reduce aggressive behavior

Child Safety

Children under 10 are bitten more often than any other age group. Most childhood bites involve the face or head. Teach children never to approach an unfamiliar dog without owner permission, never to disturb a sleeping or eating pet, and to stay still rather than run if a strange dog approaches.

Animal Bites and Zoonotic Diseases

Several diseases pass from animals to humans through bites or scratches. The four most clinically important are rabies, tetanus, cat scratch fever, and capnocytophaga.

Rabies

Rabies is a viral infection of the nervous system that is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear. The CDC reports that rabies is 100 percent preventable when post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is given before symptoms develop.

Bats are the most common rabies source in the United States, followed by raccoons, skunks, and foxes. Any bite from a wild animal, a stray of unknown vaccination status, or an animal acting strangely should be evaluated for rabies risk and possible PEP.

Tetanus

Tetanus bacteria live in soil and dust and can enter through any wound that breaks the skin, including animal bites. The CDC notes that adults need a tetanus booster every 10 years, and after 5 years for dirty or severe wounds.

If you cannot remember when your last tetanus shot was, plan to get one after a bite.

Cat Scratch Fever (Bartonella)

Caused by the Bartonella henselae bacteria, cat scratch fever produces fever, swollen lymph nodes near the scratch or bite, and fatigue. Most cases resolve on their own, but immunocompromised people can develop more serious complications.

Capnocytophaga

This bacterium lives in dog and cat mouths. In healthy people it causes mild infections, but in people without a spleen, with alcohol use disorder, or with weakened immune systems, capnocytophaga can cause severe sepsis. Tell your doctor if you have any of these risk factors after a bite.

When to Seek Emergency Care for Animal Bites

Some bites need immediate ER evaluation. Call 911 or come directly to the ER for any of these:

  • Deep puncture wounds or wounds where you can see exposed bone, tendon, or muscle
  • Severe bleeding that does not stop with 10 minutes of firm pressure
  • Bites on the face, hands, feet, or near a joint, which carry higher risk for permanent damage and infection
  • Bites from wild animals (raccoon, skunk, bat, fox, coyote) or any animal that may have rabies
  • Bites from a stray animal with unknown vaccination status
  • Any bite where the animal was acting strangely (excessive aggression, unusual tameness, paralysis)
  • Signs of infection developing in the days after the bite (red streaks, fever, increasing pain)
  • People with weakened immune systems or no spleen, who face higher infection risk from any bite

For broader emergency-recognition guidance, see our medical emergency signs guide.

Get Emergency Care for Animal Bites at ER of Lufkin

If you or a loved one has been bitten by an animal, especially a wild animal, an unknown stray, or one acting strangely, call 911 or come directly to ER of Lufkin. Our experienced emergency physicians and nurses provide evaluation and treatment 24 hours a day.

Our emergency department offers wound irrigation and debridement, tetanus vaccination, rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), IV antibiotics, and surgical consultation when needed. Walk-ins are welcome.

Phone: (936) 427-1313
Email: info@eroflufkin.com
Hours: Open 24 hours, 7 days a week
Get directions on Google Maps

FAQs

What are the signs of infection after an animal bite?

Watch for increasing redness, swelling, or warmth at the bite site. Pus or yellow drainage, red streaks extending from the wound, fever, chills, or worsening pain are other warning signs.

Get evaluated immediately if any of these appear.

Should I get a tetanus shot after an animal bite?

Often yes. Adults need a booster every 10 years, and after 5 years for dirty or severe wounds. If you cannot remember when your last tetanus shot was, plan to get one. The ER or your primary care doctor can administer it.

When does an animal bite need stitches?

Bites that gape open, bleed heavily, expose tissue, or are on the face often need stitches or other wound closure. Cat bites and many dog bites on the hand are usually NOT closed with stitches.

Closure can trap bacteria, so these bites are left open with antibiotics instead.

Are cat bites more dangerous than dog bites?

Yes, in terms of infection risk. Cat bites become infected about half the time because cat teeth create deep, narrow puncture wounds that trap bacteria. Dog bites are more likely to cause visible lacerations but have lower infection rates.

How soon after an animal bite should I see a doctor?

Within 6 hours for any bite that breaks the skin, sooner if the wound is deep, on the face or hand, or from a wild or unknown animal. Mayo Clinic data shows wound care within 6 hours dramatically lowers infection risk.

What is rabies post-exposure prophylaxis?

PEP is a series of vaccinations and a one-time dose of rabies immune globulin given after a possible rabies exposure. It is highly effective when started before symptoms appear.

Once rabies symptoms develop, the disease is nearly always fatal, so PEP is treated as a medical emergency.

title.raw: Blood Clot Treatment: A Complete Guide to Care and Recovery
title.rendered: Blood Clot Treatment: A Complete Guide to Care and Recovery

content.raw:
The untreated blood clots may be life-threatening, but timely detection and appropriate management can save lives. Whether your loved one or you just got a new diagnosis or just have to learn how to avoid future clots, you only need to know the treatment that works out and the ones to avoid, all of which depend on your knowledge. This guide discusses the most complex treatments and safety measures, the most significant steps to implement in the hospital and at home, based on the questions that are most frequently asked by patients in a case.

What Is the Best Treatment for Blood Clots?

Treating a blood clot involves preventing it from enlarging, causing new ones, and letting your body destroy it on its own.

How Do You Flush Out Blood Clots?

A clot can not really be flushed away by fluids or home therapies. It is dissolved by your body, and once suitable treatment is undertaken, it is dissolved in the body over time. The CDC recommends Blood thinners (anticoagulants) such as heparin or warfarin as primary therapy to prevent the growth of the clot during natural healing.

Which Medicine Is Best for Blood Clots?

According to MedlinePlus, heparin injections usually form the first line of immediate action, followed by warfarin oral anticoagulant, or newer direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as apixaban or rivaroxaban.

How to Treat a Blood Clot in the Arm

NHLBI states that Upper-extremity clots are managed using the same blood thinners as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the legs. A catheter procedure might be required in some exceptional circumstances to dissolve or manually remove the clot.

How Can I Make My Blood Clot Heal Faster?

As stated by Stop the Clot, you cannot accelerate the decomposition of clots. Still, you may help the wound heal: take all medication as prescribed, maintain hydration, and walk regularly as suggested by your doctor.

Can Your Body Get Rid of Blood Clots on Its Own?

Indeed, most clots reduce on their own following anticoagulation therapy. As the CDC advises, it should never self-resolve unless under medical supervision.

What Are the Five Warning Signs of a Blood Clot?

MedlinePlus states that swelling, pain/tenderness, all-over warmth, red or discoloured, sudden dyspnea (in case of the clot moving to the lungs) are to be observed.

What Not to Do When You Have a Blood Clot

Some of our habits may worsen or slow healing.

Should You Walk or Rest with a Blood Clot?

Stop the Clot explains that doctor-approved walking is generally encouraged to improve circulation, but avoid strenuous exercise until cleared. 

What Can Make Blood Clots Worse?

The CDC indicates that missing doses of blood thinners, smoking, dehydration, and excessive sitting are all of great susceptibility to the growth of clots.

What Are the Best Things to Do When You Have a Blood Clot?

According to NHLBI, take medicines on schedule, use compression stockings when advised, engage in activity with medical care, and attend all follow-up visits.

How to Treat a Blood Clot in the Leg During Pregnancy

According to MedlinePlus, pregnant patients are typically given low-molecular-weight heparin that is not able to penetrate the placenta and is therefore free of side effects on the baby

What Is the Best Position to Sleep in with Blood Clots?

Elevate the affected limb slightly to help reduce swelling, but maintain a position that feels comfortable and does not restrict blood flow.

Does Drinking Water Help Dissolve Blood Clots?

According to Stop the Clot, hydration enables normal circulation, but it is unable to dissolve an existing clot. Water aids no cure but is preventive.

Will You Be Hospitalized for a Blood Clot?

Hospitalization is determined by the size of the clot and its position, as well as the risk of complications.

How Long Are You Hospitalized for a Blood Clot?

According to the CDC, the average length of stay is one to seven days based on the severity and IV medication requirements.

Will the ER Send You Home with a Blood Clot?

Some stable patients can go home the same day with oral anticoagulants and close outpatient monitoring.

How Does a Hospital Treat a Blood Clot?

According to NHLBI, treatment may include IV heparin, transition to oral blood thinners, and, in severe cases, thrombolytic (“clot-busting”) therapy or a catheter-directed procedure.

How Likely Are You to Survive a Blood Clot?

According to MedlinePlus, survival rates are high with early treatment. Pulmonary embolism may be lethal otherwise, hence the necessity to provide immediate treatment.

How Serious Is a Suspected Blood Clot?

It should be considered an emergency in medicine. Later care worsens the chances of lung thrombus or stroke.

How Long Does It Take to Remove a Blood Clot?

Stop the Clot even after the symptoms disappear, it might take weeks or months clot to be restored to the normal condition.

What Can You Do at Home for a Blood Clot?

Self-care supports medical treatment and prevents new clots.

What Is the Fastest Way to Dissolve a Blood Clot?

CDC says there is no instant solution. Prescription anticoagulants remain the fastest and safest method.

What Can I Take Over the Counter for Blood Clots?

A clot cannot be treated by any over-the-counter medication. Prescription blood thinners should not be taken as supplements or aspirin.

What Drinks Help Dissolve Blood Clots?

Although there are no beverages that dissolve a clot, hydration with water, herbal teas, or low-calorie fluids is beneficial to the general well-being of the vascular system.

Can Aspirin Dissolve a Blood Clot?

MedlinePlus states that aspirin helps prevent platelets from clumping but does not break down an existing clot.

Can a Blood Clot Resolve on Its Own?

Yes, many clots shrink naturally after proper treatment, but medical supervision is essential to ensure safety.

Don’t wait if you suspect a blood clot

If you notice sudden leg swelling, sharp chest pain, or difficulty breathing, go straight to the ER of Lufkin. Our experienced emergency physicians provide immediate, compassionate care with advanced imaging and clot-stabilizing treatments, day or night. Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

How long does it take for a blood clot to dissolve with treatment?

Most clots shrink within a few days of blood-thinner therapy but may take weeks to months to fully dissolve.

Can a blood clot go away on its own without medication?

Sometimes, but it’s unsafe to wait; untreated clots can grow or travel to the lungs, so prompt medical care is essential.

What is the best medicine for treating blood clots?

Anticoagulants (blood thinners) such as heparin, warfarin, or DOACs like apixaban are standard treatments.

Is aspirin effective for dissolving blood clots?

No. Aspirin can help prevent new clots, but cannot break down an existing one.

Does ER of Lufkin treat blood clots?

Yes. The ER of Lufkin team is equipped with advanced diagnostic tools and can start critical treatments such as anticoagulation therapy or rapid transfer to a vascular specialist right away.

Stop the Clot explains that doctor-approved walking is generally encouraged to improve circulation, but avoid strenuous exercise until cleared. 

What Can Make Blood Clots Worse?

The CDC indicates that missing doses of blood thinners, smoking, dehydration, and excessive sitting are all of great susceptibility to the growth of clots.

What Are the Best Things to Do When You Have a Blood Clot?

According to NHLBI, take medicines on schedule, use compression stockings when advised, engage in activity with medical care, and attend all follow-up visits.

How to Treat a Blood Clot in the Leg During Pregnancy

According to MedlinePlus, pregnant patients are typically given low-molecular-weight heparin that is not able to penetrate the placenta and is therefore free of side effects on the baby

What Is the Best Position to Sleep in with Blood Clots?

Elevate the affected limb slightly to help reduce swelling, but maintain a position that feels comfortable and does not restrict blood flow.

Does Drinking Water Help Dissolve Blood Clots?

According to Stop the Clot, hydration enables normal circulation, but it is unable to dissolve an existing clot. Water aids no cure but is preventive.

Will You Be Hospitalized for a Blood Clot?

Hospitalization is determined by the size of the clot and its position, as well as the risk of complications.

How Long Are You Hospitalized for a Blood Clot?

According to the CDC, the average length of stay is one to seven days based on the severity and IV medication requirements.

Will the ER Send You Home with a Blood Clot?

Some stable patients can go home the same day with oral anticoagulants and close outpatient monitoring.

How Does a Hospital Treat a Blood Clot?

According to NHLBI, treatment may include IV heparin, transition to oral blood thinners, and, in severe cases, thrombolytic (“clot-busting”) therapy or a catheter-directed procedure.

How Likely Are You to Survive a Blood Clot?

According to MedlinePlus, survival rates are high with early treatment. Pulmonary embolism may be lethal otherwise, hence the necessity to provide immediate treatment.

How Serious Is a Suspected Blood Clot?

It should be considered an emergency in medicine. Later care worsens the chances of lung thrombus or stroke.

How Long Does It Take to Remove a Blood Clot?

Stop the Clot even after the symptoms disappear, it might take weeks or months clot to be restored to the normal condition.

What Can You Do at Home for a Blood Clot?

Self-care supports medical treatment and prevents new clots.

What Is the Fastest Way to Dissolve a Blood Clot?

CDC says there is no instant solution. Prescription anticoagulants remain the fastest and safest method.

What Can I Take Over the Counter for Blood Clots?

A clot cannot be treated by any over-the-counter medication. Prescription blood thinners should not be taken as supplements or aspirin.

What Drinks Help Dissolve Blood Clots?

Although there are no beverages that dissolve a clot, hydration with water, herbal teas, or low-calorie fluids is beneficial to the general well-being of the vascular system.

Can Aspirin Dissolve a Blood Clot?

MedlinePlus states that aspirin helps prevent platelets from clumping but does not break down an existing clot.

Can a Blood Clot Resolve on Its Own?

Yes, many clots shrink naturally after proper treatment, but medical supervision is essential to ensure safety.

Don’t wait if you suspect a blood clot

If you notice sudden leg swelling, sharp chest pain, or difficulty breathing, go straight to the ER of Lufkin. Our experienced emergency physicians provide immediate, compassionate care with advanced imaging and clot-stabilizing treatments, day or night.

Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands.

Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313

Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

How long does it take for a blood clot to dissolve with treatment?

Most clots shrink within a few days of blood-thinner therapy but may take weeks to months to fully dissolve.

Can a blood clot go away on its own without medication?

Sometimes, but it’s unsafe to wait; untreated clots can grow or travel to the lungs, so prompt medical care is essential.

What is the best medicine for treating blood clots?

Anticoagulants (blood thinners) such as heparin, warfarin, or DOACs like apixaban are standard treatments.

Is aspirin effective for dissolving blood clots?

No. Aspirin can help prevent new clots, but cannot break down an existing one.

Does ER of Lufkin treat blood clots?

Yes. The ER of Lufkin team is equipped with advanced diagnostic tools and can start critical treatments such as anticoagulation therapy or rapid transfer to a vascular specialist right away.

title.raw: COVID Testing: What You Need to Know Today
title.rendered: COVID Testing: What You Need to Know Today

content.raw:
The most acute period of the pandemic has passed, but COVID-19 has not disappeared. Cases of people falling ill are still not stopping, and new variants are kept appearing. Testing is among the surest methods of self-protection, family, and community. It solves the very important question: “Am I contagious? The CDC recommends testing in case you become sick, you were in close contact with a person with COVID-19, or you have an event with people who may be at risk of severe illness. The WHO underlines the fact that timely and correct testing can be used to diagnose cases early and stop their further transmission. This guide will be divided into when to test, the type of tests available, where to locate the tests, and the most frequently asked questions by people today.

How Soon Should You Test for COVID if You Have Symptoms?

How long should I have had symptoms before testing?

Don’t wait if you feel good and have symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, and loss of taste and smell. You should test immediately. Timely testing would give you the best chance of early COVID-19 diagnosis, and begin precautions (masking or isolation).

How long after exposure does it take to test positive?

COVID-19 has an incubation period. According to the CDC, on average, it takes 3-5 days after exposure before there is sufficient virus to accumulate to give a positive test. There is the risk that early testing can yield a false negative, and retesting is advisable in case the symptoms manifest later.

What is the best time to take a COVID-19 test?

  • If you have symptoms: Test immediately.
  • If you’ve been exposed but don’t have symptoms: Test on day 5 following exposure.
  • If you’re preparing for a gathering, test the same day as the event for the most accurate reassurance.

Can you have symptoms but test negative at first?

Yes. Other times, your body presents the symptoms even before the virus can be detected. In case you become ill, but you are negative, the CDC suggests that you should isolate and retest within 24-48 hours. The second test will prove that you really have COVID or another disease, such as the flu or allergies.

Can You Still Get a Free COVID Test in Washington State?

Are free COVID tests still available?

Federal free-test programs have generally ceased, but in most states, such as Washington, test kits are still offered by health departments, libraries, and community health centers. Your local public health site is worth a visit to see where there are currently distribution points.

Can seniors get free COVID tests?

Yes. At-home COVID tests are covered in many plans of Medicare Advantage and Part D. Free kits are also distributed in senior centers and community programs in some cases. Elderly people ought to inquire with their doctor or pharmacist about eligibility.

Do I have to pay for a COVID test?

Payment depends on your insurance coverage and the reason for the test.
  • Medical need (e.g., symptoms or exposure): Most insurers cover testing.
  • Non-medical need (e.g., travel, employer request): You may need to pay out of pocket.

Do expired COVID tests work?

The FDA has re-expired most brands after additional stability testing. Review the new list on the FDA site before disposing of a test. A test that has expired can remain valid for many months to come.

How long am I contagious with COVID-19?

Most people are most contagious from 1–2 days before symptoms start through the first 5 days of illness. Others might be left contagious for 10 days. Testing may be used to ensure that it is safe to resume normal activities.

Is There a Current Test for COVID?

Are new COVID tests available?

Yes. Manufacturers also keep updating the test designs to identify the variants circulating.

Can current COVID tests detect the new variant?

The CDC claims that the majority of FDA-approved antigen and PCR tests are effective in identifying the predominant variants, but sensitivity can be slightly low.

Do COVID tests work now?

Absolutely. Rapid antigen tests can be a bit less sensitive in early infection, although they are also an important instrument, particularly when repeated on many days.

Should you even test for COVID anymore?

Yes. Testing still matters. It helps you protect high-risk loved ones, guides decisions about antiviral treatment, and prevents outbreaks in schools and workplaces.

How accurate are COVID tests now?

  • PCR tests: The gold standard, with very high accuracy. Results typically return in 1–2 days.
  • Rapid antigen tests: Convenient and fast (15–30 minutes), but less sensitive. Their accuracy improves when taken several times over a few days.

How do I know if I have COVID?

The only reliable way is to test. COVID symptoms overlap with flu, RSV, and allergies. A test provides clarity and helps you take the right precautions.

Can I Get a COVID Test at CVS?

Can you buy COVID tests anymore?

Yes. At-home antigen tests are widely available at CVS, Walgreens, Walmart, and online retailers like Amazon.

Are pharmacies giving away free tests?

Some pharmacies still partner with state or local health programs to distribute free tests. Supplies vary, so it’s best to call your local CVS or pharmacy.

Do COVID tests show results immediately?

Rapid antigen tests give results in 15–30 minutes. PCR tests must be processed in a lab, usually taking 24–48 hours.

Are COVID tests available on the shelf?

Yes, most pharmacies keep them stocked in the cold and flu section. You can walk in and purchase them over the counter.

Are new COVID tests available?

Yes, testing technology has advanced. At the ER of Lufkin, we use cutting-edge diagnostics like the 22-panel Biofire Respiratory Panel. This panel not only detects COVID-19 but also identifies a broad range of respiratory pathogens, offering a faster and more accurate diagnosis for patients. This advanced technology helps us pinpoint whether your symptoms are due to COVID-19, the flu, or another illness, ensuring you get the right treatment quickly.

Can current COVID tests detect the new variant?

Yes, the 22-panel Biofire Respiratory Panel detects COVID-19 and most major variants circulating in the community. This test is highly sensitive and provides results on time, so you can make informed decisions about your health and safety.

Protect Yourself and Others

COVID-19 may not dominate headlines anymore, but it still poses a risk, especially for older adults, people with chronic conditions, and those with weakened immune systems. If you feel sick, have been exposed, or want peace of mind before visiting family, get tested today.  ER of Lufkin is open 24/7 and offers rapid COVID-19 testing along with full emergency care. Our compassionate team is here to give you quick answers and expert support whenever you need it. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

When should I test for COVID if I have symptoms?

Test immediately, and if negative, retest in 24–48 hours.

How soon after exposure should I test?

On day 5 after exposure, or sooner if you develop symptoms.

Are expired COVID tests still valid?

Many have extended expiration dates; check the FDA website before discarding.

Where can I still get free COVID tests in Washington?

Local health departments, libraries, and community health clinics.

Do COVID tests detect new variants?

Yes, most FDA-authorized tests detect currently circulating variants.

Does ER of Lufkin test for COVID?

Yes. ER of Lufkin provides COVID-19 testing as part of its comprehensive emergency care services.

title.raw: Dehydration Treatment: How to Rehydrate Safely and Quickly
title.rendered: Dehydration Treatment: How to Rehydrate Safely and Quickly

content.raw:
Most people associate the process of dehydration with hot days of summer or exhaustive exercise. However, the reality is that everyone can become dehydrated at any given time. Even a small amount of fluid loss will affect mood, focus, and energy. Otherwise, NIH reports that dehydration could result in some severe health effects, particularly among children, older adults, and individuals with chronic conditions. The good news? Having a fluid electrolyte imbalance can be properly used to cure most incidences of dehydration. In this guide, we will break it all down into what you must know, including the quickest fixes and which foods to avoid, and when you should go to an emergency.

What Is the Best Remedy for Dehydration?

The Fastest Way to Fix Dehydration

According to MedlinePlus, fluids and electrolytes can be replaced to reverse dehydration the fastest, even though it demands considerable time. Plain water is effective in light forms of dehydration, but the oral rehydration solutions (ORS) are the best when dealing with moderate dehydration. The quickest and safest treatment for severe dehydration, particularly when one is not able to drink, is through intravenous (IV) fluids is normally administered in a hospital.

Three Warning Signs of Dehydration

Early detection matters. Watch for:
  • Thirst and dry mouth
  • Dark yellow urine or reduced urination
  • Lightheadedness or dizziness
These are red flags that your body urgently needs hydration.

How to Treat Dehydration in Kids

Children are more susceptible due to the fact that their bodies lose water more quickly as a result of their small size. The American Red Cross focuses on the application of oral rehydration salts, such as Pedialyte, as an alternative to soda or fruit juices, which compounds the diarrhea and fluid loss. Meanwhile, call the doctor if the child sinks the eyes, is unable to vomit continuously, or is unusually drowsy.

What Drink Will Hydrate You the Fastest?

  • Water is the foundation.
  • Electrolyte-rich sports drinks or ORS are better if you’ve lost fluids through sweating, vomiting, or diarrhea.
  • Coconut water can also be a natural option for mild dehydration.
  • Avoid alcohol and caffeine, which can worsen dehydration.

What Home Remedy Is Good for Dehydration?

Much more basic, a home option: a mixture of 1/2 teaspoon salt and 6 teaspoons sugar added to 1 liter of clean water. This formulates a simple oral rehydrating solution in the absence of commercial ORS. Stopping by adding water-filled fruits such as watermelon, cucumber, or oranges is also helpful for hydration purposes.

What Not to Eat When You’re Dehydrated

Stay out of foods that contain high amounts of sodium and refined sugar, such as chips, instant noodles, and processed snacks. These pull the water out of your cells and decelerate recovery.

What Is the Fastest Way to Hydrate Your Body?

What Hydrates a Body Faster Than Water?

Water is the most natural thing technically, yet, in medical conditions, ORS or IV fluids are more effective than plain water since they replace the lost electrolytes as well as hydration.

Five Warning Signs of Dehydration

In addition to thirst and dizziness, severe dehydration may bring:
  • Rapid heartbeat
  • Fatigue or confusion
  • Sunken eyes
  • Very little or no urination
  • Cool, clammy skin

What Is the Fastest Way to Rehydrate Your Body?

Drinking water or an electrolyte beverage over the course of several hours is safest for most people. Drinking large volumes of water at once can result in stomach problems or too rapid electrolyte loss.

What Drink Hydrates You Instantly?

Although none of the drinks has an immediate effect, IV fluids have the quickest effect. Balanced electrolyte solutions are the other best option to use in the case of home recovery.

What Drink Is the Most Hydrating?

Interestingly, NIH recommends milk and ORS to hydrate more than water, as they remain in the body longer, since their composition is well-balanced.

Does Warm Water Hydrate Faster?

This is a common myth. Warm water, cold water, or room temperature water all hydrate well- it is up to comfort and taste.

What Not to Eat When Dehydrated

Should You Eat If You’re Dehydrated?

Yes, but keep it light, food with high water content: fruits, vegetables, broths. Salt or fat-heavy meals will add to the water requirements of your body.

What Makes Dehydration Worse?

  • Alcohol and caffeinated drinks
  • Salty and fried foods
  • Excessive protein without fluids

What Should You Avoid When You Are Dehydrated?

Avoid processed snacks, sugary sodas, and high-salt condiments. They can worsen fluid imbalance.

How Long Does It Take to Recover From Dehydration?

  • Mild cases: a few hours with steady fluid intake.
  • Moderate cases: 24–48 hours with ORS and rest.
  • Severe cases: may require hospitalization and IV fluids for days.

Does Dehydration Cause Diarrhea?

Can I Get Diarrhea From Being Dehydrated?

No. Diarrhea causes dehydration, not the other way around.

Does Diarrhea Mean Not Enough Water?

Not directly, but diarrhea rapidly strips your body of water and electrolytes.

How Does Dehydration Affect Bowel Movements?

Dehydration is more likely to cause constipation—the body pulls extra water from the colon, making stools dry and hard.

Can Drinking a Lot of Water Stop Diarrhea?

No, but it prevents dehydration during diarrheal illness. Pair water with ORS to replace lost sodium and potassium.

What Can Be Mistaken for Dehydration?

  • Heat exhaustion
  • Low blood sugar
  • Anxiety or panic attacks
  • Certain infections or medication side effects
When in doubt, it’s safest to consult a healthcare provider.

Staying Hydrated at the FIFA World Cup 2026 in Texas

The FIFA World Cup 2026 is coming to Texas, with matches running from June 11 through July 19 at NRG Stadium in Houston and Dallas Stadium (AT&T Stadium) in Arlington, which hosts nine games, including a semifinal on July 14. That puts the world's biggest sporting event right in the middle of peak Texas summer heat, and for fans traveling from East Texas, the drive, the tailgate, and the watch party can be just as dehydrating as the match itself. Lufkin sits squarely between the two host cities, making it a natural stop for anyone road-tripping to a game. Whether you're heading south to Houston or north to Arlington, a little hydration planning before kickoff can be the difference between a great day and a trip to the emergency room.

Should You Hydrate Before You Get to the Stadium?

Yes, and this is the mistake most fans make. By the time you feel thirsty in the Texas summer, you're already roughly 2% dehydrated, which is enough to cause fatigue, headaches, and irritability before the first whistle. Hydration isn't something you fix in the parking lot; it's something you start the day before. Drink water steadily in the 24 hours leading up to the match rather than chugging a large amount right before you leave.

What Should You Pack for a World Cup Match Day?

A few simple habits go a long way in the heat:
  • Drink water on a schedule, not on thirst. Aim for steady sips throughout the morning and during the drive.
  • Add electrolytes for long, hot days. An ORS or a balanced electrolyte drink replaces the sodium and potassium you lose through sweat more effectively than water alone when you're out for hours.
  • Go easy on alcohol and caffeine. Game-day beers and energy drinks both pull water from your body and speed up dehydration.
  • Eat water-rich foods. Watermelon, oranges, and cucumber, before you head out, add hydration on top of what you drink.
  • Dress for the heat. Light, breathable clothing and a hat reduce how hard your body has to work to stay cool.

Aren't the Texas Stadiums Air-Conditioned?

They are both NRG Stadium and Dallas Stadium are climate-controlled, so the seats inside stay comfortable. But the real risk isn't the 90 minutes of play. It's the hours spent outside it: tailgating in the parking lot, waiting in security lines, walking from distant lots, and sitting in traffic on the way home. That's when heat and humidity quietly drain you, especially in a city like Houston, where high humidity stops sweat from evaporating and prevents your body from cooling itself properly.

How Do Watch Parties Cause Dehydration?

You don't have to be inside the stadium to be at risk. Outdoor watch parties, backyard gatherings, and fan fests across East Texas mean long afternoons in the sun, often paired with alcohol and salty snacks, a combination that worsens fluid loss. If you're hosting or attending one, keep water and electrolyte drinks within easy reach, take shade breaks, and watch for early warning signs in kids and older guests, who dehydrate faster than healthy adults.

When Should World Cup Fans Seek Emergency Care?

Mild dehydration usually resolves with fluids and rest. But if you or someone in your group experiences a rapid heartbeat, confusion, fainting, sunken eyes, cool and clammy skin, or can't keep fluids down, don't wait it out; these are signs of severe dehydration or heat illness that need medical attention.

Take Care of Your Hydration Health

Dehydration can sneak up on anyone, whether from illness, exercise, or simply forgetting to drink enough water. Mild dehydration can usually be managed at home with fluids and rest, but severe dehydration is a medical emergency. If you or a loved one experiences confusion, rapid heartbeat, fainting, or an inability to keep fluids down, don’t wait. Visit the ER of Lufkin for immediate, compassionate care. Our team is available 24/7 to provide advanced treatment, including IV hydration and monitoring, so you can recover safely. Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313 Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What is the best way to quickly fix dehydration?

Drink water or an ORS; use IV fluids for severe cases.

What are the early warning signs of dehydration?

Thirst, dizziness, fatigue, and dark-colored urine.

Can children recover from dehydration at home?

Yes, with ORS, unless they show severe symptoms (then seek care).

What foods and drinks should I avoid when dehydrated?

Salty snacks, processed foods, alcohol, and caffeine.

How long does it take to recover from dehydration?

Mild: a few hours. Severe: days, often with IV treatment.

Does ER of Lufkin treat dehydration?

Yes. ER of Lufkin provides 24/7 emergency care for dehydration, from mild cases that may need fluids and monitoring to severe dehydration requiring IV treatment.

Can I just drink water once I get into the stadium?

No. By the time you feel thirsty in a Texas summer, you are already roughly 2% dehydrated, which can lead to fatigue and headaches before kickoff.

Is the humidity in Houston really that dangerous?

Yes. High humidity prevents sweat from evaporating, which is your body’s primary way of cooling down. In Houston, you can become dehydrated even if you aren’t "dripping" sweat.
